results.title: ClickFix Lures Deploy ChainScript RAT Using Polygon to Rotate C2 Infrastructure
results.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
results.content:
Threat actors are leveraging ClickFix-like lures to deliver a previously undocumented remote access trojan (RAT) called ChainScript.
"ChainScript has appeared under multiple build names, including ComponentTask33, UpdateDigital, HostShared, and OrchidViolet66, while presenting itself as Spotify, Zoom Workplace, and Microsoft Teams software," Blackpoint Adversary Pursuit Group (APG) researchers Sam Decker, Andi Ursry, and Nevan Beal said.
Like many malware families observed in recent months, ChainScript employs an EtherHiding-style command-and-control (C2) discovery technique that makes use of a Polygon smart contract to locate its active WebSocket infrastructure.
ChainScript is a full-featured RAT that provides extensive remote access to the operator, including interactive CMD and PowerShell, file operations, screenshot capture, payload deployment, cryptocurrency wallet enumeration (both desktop apps and browser extensions), and remote JavaScript execution.
The starting point of the attack chain is a ClickFix lure that leads to the download and execution of a malicious Windows installer using "msiexec.exe." The installer ("ComponentTask33-4d14e6ac.msi"), disguised as Spotify, deploys the Node.js runtime and launches the ChainScript JavaScript agent through hidden PowerShell and VBScript stages.
The PowerShell script drops various components, namely, the runtime, agent source, configuration, and other auxiliary binaries, across different Microsoft-looking paths in the "%LOCALAPPDATA%" folder. The VBScript serves as the main launcher for ChainScript.
The running agent then establishes user level persistence through a scheduled task with a Registry Run key fallback. Upon execution, ChainScript connects to the C2 server over WebSockets and retrieves additional tasking, giving the threat actor direct control over the compromised system. The supported commands also allow it to self-update and remove persistence.
The findings illustrate how threat actors are increasingly adopting a flexible decentralized infrastructure as a way to resist takedown efforts and ensure uninterrupted operations.
"ChainScript reflects an emerging pattern of malware using development frameworks and blockchain-based C2 discovery to enable infrastructure rotation and complicate traditional indicator-based detection," Blackpoint said. "By separating backend discovery from the malware itself and using the Polygon contract as an external resolver, the operator can redirect infected hosts to new infrastructure while retaining the same implant and reconnect workflow."
ClickFix, a Way for Mac and Windows Users to Infect Themselves
The disclosure comes as threat actors compromised HBO Max's official Reddit account ("u/hbomax") and abused it to push malicious ads that launched ClickFix attacks to infect Windows and macOS devices with information-stealing malware. The activity has been codenamed PasteSwitch by Hudson Rock and ADAMnetworks. It's not known how the account was breached, and how many people clicked on these fake ads and how many were compromised as a result.
On macOS, PasteSwitch has been found to deliver MacSync, Atomic macOS Stealer (AMOS), and fake cryptocurrency wallet applications designed to steal recovery phrases. The Windows branch, on the other hand, distributes Amatera Stealer and cryptocurrency clippers like AnimateClipper and ZigClipper. In all, the verified Reddit account served 108 malicious ads over a 48-hour period in mid-September 2026.
According to data shared by Seqrite Labs, MacSync infections have concentrated in the U.S., followed by the U.K., Germany, Japan, Canada, France, Singapore, Australia, India, and the Netherlands. "MacSync campaigns primarily target regions with widespread macOS enterprise use, tech and software development sectors, and active cryptocurrency or Web3 communities," researcher Chandra Kant Bauri said.
"The threat actors utilized highly polished assets to establish trust before delivering the malicious payload," Hudson Rock said. "By hijacking a verified corporate account, they bypassed the initial skepticism many users apply to internet advertisements."
The findings dovetail with another ClickFix campaign that employs a fake Codex download experience surfaced via search results to lead users to bogus Google Sites pages and trick macOS users into pasting a malicious command into Terminal, resulting in the execution of Atomic Stealer. Visitors using non-Mac devices are served a harmless decoy page.
"The copied Terminal command first retrieves a shell-script loader: the first stage," Cato Networks said. "This loader contains an embedded blob that it decodes and executes with eval, producing the second-stage shell script. The second stage then records execution and retrieves the final, third-stage Mach-O payload."
The cybersecurity company described the activity as part of a broader pattern of attacks that employ trusted services and large language model (LLM) shared chats to serve fake installation instructions, while bypassing browser warnings, URL inspection, and Safe Browsing heuristics.
In a report published last month, Microsoft said it observed a macOS ClickFix campaign propagating MacSync and Atomic Stealer using a cluster of no less than 250 look-alike domains.
"The campaign evolved from broadly serving ClickFix lures to using a server-side browser-fingerprinting gate that shows the lure primarily to visitors whose environment appears consistent with a genuine macOS browser," it said. "This cloaking limits visibility for crawlers, sandboxes, and some automated analysis workflows."
results.summary:
Cybersecurity researchers have identified a new remote access trojan called ChainScript that uses deceptive ClickFix lures and blockchain-based command-and-control infrastructure to compromise Windows systems globally.

### Key Points
- ChainScript disguises itself as legitimate software like Spotify, Zoom, and Microsoft Teams to trick users into executing malicious Windows installers.
- The malware utilizes a Polygon smart contract for command-and-control discovery, allowing operators to rotate infrastructure and evade detection.
- Capabilities include remote command execution, file manipulation, screenshot capture, and the theft of cryptocurrency wallet data from browsers and desktop applications.
- Attackers are increasingly using ClickFix tactics, including the recent hijacking of a verified HBO Max Reddit account to distribute information-stealing malware.
- Campaigns targeting macOS users, such as those distributing MacSync and Atomic Stealer, are leveraging browser-fingerprinting to bypass security crawlers and sandboxes.

### Why it Matters
These campaigns demonstrate a shift toward decentralized infrastructure and the abuse of trusted platforms to bypass traditional security heuristics. By leveraging blockchain technology and verified corporate accounts, threat actors are significantly increasing the difficulty of detecting and neutralizing persistent malware threats.

results.title: [Podcast] Customer Experience Psychology: How to Build a Memorable Brand with Si Elliot
results.author: Jacob Cass
results.content:
What makes a customer experience memorable?
In this episode, Jacob Cass & Matt Davies speak with customer experience expert and author Si Elliott about the psychology behind how people experience, perceive and remember brands.
Drawing from his book, Customer Experience Thinking, Si explains how behavioural science can help brands create stronger customer relationships. They explore the role of expectations, emotion, identity, effort, personalisation and control, along with the small details that can shape an entire experience.
They also unpack some of the behavioural biases every brand strategist should understand, including loss aversion, framing, anchoring, social proof, the paradox of choice and the peak-end rule.
You’ll discover:
- Why a customer’s memory of an experience may matter more than the experience itself
- How first impressions influence everything that follows
- Why offering more choice can make an experience worse
- The difference between being personal and being personalised
- How emotion and identity shape brand preference
- Where AI can improve customer experience and where humans should lead
If you want to create brand experiences that feel more human, valuable and memorable, this conversation will change how you think about every customer interaction.

Transcript
Hello, folks, welcome to this episode of JUST Branding. Brands spend an absolutely enormous amount of time thinking about how they look, what they say, how they present themselves to the world. But we know that ultimately brands are experienced by human beings, by end consumers. And we know that those human beings sometimes, I would pretty much say all the time, are not really rational in the way that they think and behave. We’re all emotional beings, influenced by context and various other key things. So we’re not robots. So if we want to manage meaning, if we want to build brands, it’s so important that we get our heads around consumer behavior, customer behavior, you could call it, and behavioral science. Today, in this episode, we are exploring a simple question. What can behavioral science teach us about creating better customer and therefore brand experiences? And we have an amazing guest to go into this subject with. Today, we’re joined by Si Elliott, a customer experience expert who spent the last two decades exploring the intersection between digital progress and human connection. Si began his career in marketing and today co-owns creative agency, Diversity, and is the founder of customer experience consultancy, Fabrics, where he combines behavioral science with practical strategy to help organizations create experiences that genuinely resonate with people. On top of that, if that wasn’t enough, he’s also an award-winning guest lecturer at Nottingham Trent University here in the UK, the University of Nottingham and the Communication University of China, as well as sitting on academic advisory boards spanning business and psychology. And perhaps most relevantly, he is the author of a new book that’s just come out this year, Customer Experience Thinking, a practical guide to using behavioral science to build deeper, more meaningful customer relationships. Si, welcome to the podcast.
Thank you for that introduction. There’s very little I can say now. I think you’ve pretty much cut off everything you’ve done.
Let’s wrap it up. Well, I think we could tuck into one small story, and that’s how we first met. Do you want to sort of, you know, open up that can of worms?
Yeah. So 2004, I think it was, our creative studio was a little bit overloaded with work. So we went out to some freelance designers here in Nottingham, and a very energetic young chap with a lot of hair arrived through the door. Did some fantastic work with us. So I can vouch that the work was very good. And we’ve been in touch ever since. And I think it’s always interesting when you have, and you’ve just reeled off a lot of things that I’ve done. And the reason I’ve done that is because I’ve been around for so long. But I think it’s really interesting when you have more than two decades of experience in a market, in an area, in a niche, to see the people that keep coming back into your, kind of revolving around your world and your ether as well, and your network. And yeah, it’s great to see what you’re doing. It’s fantastic to meet Jacob as well. And I’ve got a few questions for Jacob a little bit later on as well. That’s a whole different thing.
Well, thanks for so much for carving out some time. I think it was a couple of years ago, we were in a Starbucks and you mentioned this book that was coming out. And now it’s here. So congratulations on launching it. We’re going to get into that. But one thing I was just going to touch on, I think what’s interesting about our connection is that, in effect, we’ve both had, I would say similar, but different approaches in our career, which is that I think we’ve gone up the value ladder, if you like, in the sense of how are we really creating stuff that has real true meaning and value for customers? And coming from the design and creative side, that’s where my career has gone more into the strategy side. And I know yours has also, and slightly differently, but ultimately kind of ending up on that side of things, which is less about, I guess, the fonts, the colors and the shiny bits, and more about the true, for you, the customer experience that really kind of generates value.
Absolutely. Yeah. And I think you touched on the book, and I’m sure we’ll chat through that a little bit. And that was certainly a labor of love. I know you’re working on one at the moment. I know, Jacob, you’ve been through that process as well. And that was a commitment device. I just told everybody I’m writing a book, because eventually, every time you see someone, they go, how are you getting on with the book? You go, yeah, I need to complete that. But, you know, an absolute curse of optimism. I thought I’d have the book done in a year. It took three years. And hopefully, there’s some value that people can get out from that. But certainly, and I know we haven’t teed up the two letters of AI yet, but we’re never going to get through this without unscathed, without talking about that. That wasn’t even in my thinking when I started the book. But it’s certainly become more important. And the point you touched on now, for anybody working agency side, a designer, people at the moment that maybe have some worries about what’s happening in the world, that moving up the value chain and adding the thinking in is absolutely critical now. It’s never been more important. It’s never. And I think when we touch on what you guys do from a brand perspective, I genuinely think that now might be the most important time in history to get brand right.
Agreed. Well, look, before we tuck in some of that stuff, let’s just start with basics, right? Because we have a varied audience that tune in and we always like to lay some groundwork first. We love definitions on the JUST Branding Podcast just to start us off. So the book’s called Customer Experience Thinking. Perhaps we could get you to give us a definition of what that is. What is customer experience thinking?
Customer experience is just the perception of feelings that people have with the interactions or the experience they have with you, your product, your service or your brand. So in simple terms, that’s all it is and it lives in the mind of the customer. So we’re trying to influence that, but fundamentally, customer experience is always from the other side of the fence and a lot of brands think about what they’re delivering as customer experience rather than what’s been received and trying to fit that on its head and walk in their shoes a little bit more.
Love that. Love that. So why is that important, do you think, to having that kind of mindset around human behavior? Why is that important to creating those experiences for businesses and brands?
Well, let’s think about why does a business exist at all? It’s to serve someone and hopefully have a value exchange where you get compensated for that service to the other side. So I think modern marketing and certainly technology has really driven us down a line of thinking about conversion, thinking about this user, that metric, and we actually need to take a step back and go, we’re actually serving people at the end of the day. A lot of the work you guys will be doing in your day jobs is not just about selling to a business, it’s serving those people within the business. And I feel in marketing, we’re losing a little bit of sight on that. Certainly with big data, certainly when we look at, you know, think about the social platforms and the ability to reach such a large audience, I feel we’re starting to lose a little bit of connection with the fact that it’s the person on the other side that we’re serving. And the brands that do it super well, and I think are gonna be really successful moving forward, are those that keep that in mind and remember, I’m here to serve you. So my book is written to hopefully serve value to you, and therefore it’s worth the money you’ve paid for it, and it creates that value. So I’ve had to write it with you in mind, not in mind of just, this is what I want to say.
Right.
How did you come to the idea of writing a book?
Well, partially, partially there’s a big personal side to it. I’ve got two young daughters, and 11 and 14, they’re digital natives. They’re growing up in a world that is so different to the world I grew up in 40 odd years ago. And I now observe that and think, well, what they’re coming into, how well is it serving them versus they’re serving it? So how much is the technology the master rather than the other way around? So I was starting to just observe this and think about the marketing industry in general, and how we’re, as I say, starting to focus more on metrics, users, conversion rate, rather than delivering out to people. And that’s been accelerated in recent years, but from the start of the book, it was really looking at that and looking at this whole trend of, we’re more connected than ever, but potentially more lonely, we’re a lot more plugged in, there’s notifications going off, I feel it. When I think about starting out in a design creative studio here in Nottingham, I was doing two or three ad campaigns a week, and I used to wait for an ISDN line to slowly tick along, and that’s great. And now I look at the speed that my team are working at, the amount of notifications going off, if you’ve got Slack, if you’ve got Teams, WhatsApp’s going off, emails, people are expecting instant answers on. Everything’s ramping up, but we’ve still got these prehistoric brains that have been formed over thousands of years, and we’re not having hardware updates with our brains as quickly as the technology is. So I’m looking at it and thinking, well, as marketeers, we have a responsibility. We fund a lot of what happens in technical development, because it’s us that is paying these platforms, wanting to have our presence on there. So it’s just thinking about that. And I was seeing a lot of clients having that frustration with, I think, the pace of optimization and wanting to build something that’s a little bit more long term. That was kind of the two things coming together, my two worlds colliding together into a, well, you’ve got an opinion on it, why don’t you start to write a book? You lecture on these things. Why don’t you get it down to paper? Because there’s also only so many conversations you can have in your lifetime. So, you know, hopefully people will pick this book up and go, I did some interesting things in there, but I’m going to move on to the next level. Like the great books I’ve read over the years, that’s part of my evolution in my thinking. I want to just be a little, one of those little ticks in someone else’s evolution along the way, where they start to maybe question things a little bit differently. And I’ve given my daughters the book and asked them to think about their decisions as consumers when they’re trying to buy stuff online as well. Love that.
And I think you’re so right, like short-termism, it can be such a drug, right, for businesses, particularly big organizations where, you know, people are so desperate to justify their existence. And if they can point towards some data somewhere, you know, it feels rational and it feels lovely. And, you know, they can kind of justify their existence when, as you say, if we lose sight of the basic thing, which is as a business, you’re there to serve someone else, you’re there to serve their need today. But if you think just about that, you’ve got a problem, because really you want to be thinking, I’m here to serve you for as long as you need me to. You know, that could be for years. And if you’ve got short-term focus and your teams are all driven, short-term, short-term, short-term, they sometimes might make a decision, which will benefit the customer and themselves in the short-term, but might damage the long-term relationship. And that, I think, is sometimes how businesses and brands get themselves into difficulty. Anyway, what I was going to say was, let’s shift gear a little bit and dive into this like full on, right? Because I know in your book you go through, which by the way, just to lend my endorsement to it, I think everybody on this who’s listening to this should definitely grab a copy. We’ll give details in a minute of where you can get it. But let’s just go into some of the principles that you outline. I think you go through like eight key principles of customer experience. So I was wondering if you’d be open to outlining those for us. And then perhaps we could dive in and unlock a couple and kind of get into some nitty gritty. Would you be open to that?
A hundred percent. Let’s start with why they principles are not rules or laws. And I’m not necessarily the most linear of characters myself. As I would imagine, many great entrepreneurs, business leaders, designers, brand strategists are as well. So the principles because, and my school reports would tell you this, I didn’t always follow the rules. But it’s something that over time that I’ve just crafted these through. So A, where we look at, consider every detail on how they work together, set, manage and exceed expectations, personalised for the individual, on their terms of putting them in control, minimising effort and stress, considering the identity and emotions, learning and building relationship over time and considering all the senses. And they’ll map against whether it’s accessible, functional or emotional or a series of those. And they just help, I think, give foundational building blocks to start planning your work around. The second half of the book dives into Behavioural Science, which takes it to a slightly different place. But that start point is things that we’ve been working with clients for years on, trying to put a little bit of a structure behind it. But I refuse to call it anything beyond principles because I don’t want to be held to it in the fullness of time. We’re allowed to rethink at some point. But certainly, you know, those are the important things that for me, when you guys are doing brand exercise, I’ve got to live up to your brand exercise, putting them through this lens of these eight principles and really testing my metal against that.
Yeah. I mean, some of them, particularly for the designers who are listening in, will be really obvious. Like that first one, consider every detail and how they work together, right? I guess from a visual perspective, a lot of people are familiar with that, but it goes beyond that, doesn’t it?
Absolutely. So as humans, we’re kind of hardwired to notice differences in environment and things that don’t quite join up. Usually that could be, and I’ll quite often talk about our prehistoric roots where you were a caveman. You’d be looking out for those queues.
You’re like the third guest recently that said that I’m a bit caveman-like. I will accept it, but I’m getting a little nervous. Carry on.
But you, evolutionary, have to look out for risks. So you look for inconsistencies, slight things, and then you go, do I trust this now? And it will be the same in any brand exercise as well, where we need to be consistent across the piece, because otherwise I won’t believe your claim. If in three places you say it, but in one place you contradict it. And that’s when I just think about wording and the things that you’re promising. Before then, I look at what you’re doing visually. So if I think about consistency visually, you say, we are an authentic people first brand, and then you’re using AI generated content on social. I don’t believe your first claim now. So consistency is really important. And I think that’s a tough one for designers, because you like novelty. You like to change things up, freshen things up. So for then someone to go, no, no, we need to be super consistent is tough. And a couple of episodes ago, I can’t remember your guest’s name now off the top of my head. But when they talk about Marlborough and then designing things in green, everything’s got to come back. Consistency is a tough one. It is a tough one because we also like novelty ourselves. And when you’re working on something so much, you forget that it’s 100% of your head space. But for the consumer, it’s that fleeting thing that they see once every four months for three seconds.
That’s a great point and I see it all the time. On a macro scale, you get a new CMO and they want to stamp their authority upon the brand, literally take it in a different direction. And again, going back to that first point, is this how we serve people well? I’m working on a big project at the moment in the US and it’s a brand relaunch and it’s going to market. We’ve got ad TV spots and all sorts going out. And I had to have a really serious conversation with the brand director over there because they asked for, in this particular project, for example, different strap lines to the end of every ad. And my position was, look, we should stick to one really strong because we want to kind of be really clear about what we stand for. And they were like, yeah, but don’t you think consumers will get bored? I was like, literally, someone’s going to see one of your ads and then not see it again or see anything to do with your brand for a day or two, right? You know, even with the best funding in the world, that’s the reality. So what we need to do is we need to think exactly this, you know, consider the detail and be really, really clear about the experience. And yeah, I think I won that one, but hey, we’ll wait and see. Time will tell. Yeah, time will tell. I also think like there’s a new rebrand that’s been echoing around the interweb of, you know, the way Coke has been refreshing there. I don’t think that they’ve gone live with it yet, there’s been some sort of leaked Coke things. And what I think is phenomenal about Coke, if you think of a brand with the longevity of say Coca-Cola, how the level of consistency around, you know, some of their key brand codes has been absolutely locked in for many, many years. The red, the ribbon, the way the can and the bottles work and all of that stuff, for years, consistency pays off. And now, yeah, they’ve tweaked a few things, typographies, tweet, you know, et cetera, et cetera. But ultimately, look at brands like that, I would say, to and consider your business, your brand and consider how frequently you’ve changed over the years. You know, a lot of B2B brands change every two, three years and they think this is what it’s about, but perhaps it’s not. Perhaps it’s about consistency.
There has been some dilemmas around with the packaging design and Coke Zero. I don’t know if you’ve seen that, but they can’t tell the difference between Coke Zero and regular Coke because the black has gone and people are picking up the wrong thing and sales are going to go down because of that. So when we talk about how things all work together, I think that is one of those things, even though the system would say to do that, we have to make a decision of like, well, does it actually help the brand and sales? I don’t know. Time will tell on that one.
And that’s where behavioral science comes in and we’re going to get to that. We’re going to get to that, but let’s keep going through these principles, right? So that was number one, consider every detail and how they work together. Number two, set, manage and exceed expectations. Kind of like, how does that work? Like that’s a tough one, right? Like how do you exceed expectations, Si?
Before we get into that, Si, I just had a question because you mentioned these, like building blocks and we want to make them usable and practical, but before we get into this, for the context of how we actually apply this, using these principles, how do you generally work with clients if you’re going through these principles and like make it usable?
So typically a client will either come in and go, let’s look at the whole of our experience, map it out, so customer journey map it right the way through. Or alternatively, they may, the spot point might be, we don’t think this bit’s working. Can we have a look at that? And then you end up expanding out from there. So they’re looking to sharpen up a certain elements they might see that they are customer satisfaction scores are through the floor. Or our NPS all of a sudden has gone massively backwards. We don’t know why. Or alternatively, we’re having this issue over here. Yeah, we used to get this response rate is now dropped down to this, or we’re seeing a higher churn in some of our customer base. So it could be any one of those. And for anybody doing this as well, you don’t always need to grab someone like me and you can just start to pick this up and look at it yourself. But I would always say where you think the problem is, is rarely where it actually is, and you have to expand it out. So they’ll be like, right, our conversion rate there is bad. Okay, why? And that does kind of come on to Matt’s next one, then, which is about set, manage and exceed expectations, which we often talk about, let’s exceed expectations. But that’s firstly, the start point actually is take a step back and go, does Jacob actually understand what is required? So let’s think about getting a mortgage. Do you know the component steps when you’re first time buyer of getting a mortgage? No, you don’t. So from the outset, we’re going to be super clear and go, right, okay, Jacob. So nine step process. First bit, you’re going to get dead excited because we’re going to tell you exactly how much money you can borrow. So then you’re going to jump over if you’re in the UK, some like right move and start searching for properties and get all excited at that point. But by the way, just to give you a heads up, there’s going to be a really boring point where we ask you to show us all your credit card statements, all your bank statements, go through that process of due diligence. That’s a real emotional low point in the process. So we’re going to have to work really hard at that point. So to start with, in a lot of purchases, we don’t have background record or history to know what we’re doing. Yeah, go to pick up a can of Coke in a local supermarket. We’ve done that handful of times, so we know what we’re doing. Although if we picked up Coke Zero, it’s a bit disappointed now because of the color scheme. But we know what we’re doing. But in a lot of cases, we don’t. If it’s the first time you’re engaging in the space, you don’t. Or alternatively, if you are the first direct, when they first came out from a banking perspective, you’re doing things differently to the other guys. You got no branches, it’s all online. So if visually you’ve got a really busy web page and someone’s already overloaded and then you want them to absorb your message or that structure to the offer that you’re putting forward, that’s going to be really tough. But when I think of context as well, I like to think if you want a nice ice cold bottle of beer, you’re going to go into the supermarket, you might pay a couple of pounds for it, maybe $3 for you, Jacob, I’m not sure. But now you’re on the beach, you’re on a holiday, it’s absolutely boiling. Someone walks up with a bucket of ice cold beers and offers you one for 10 pounds, you’re probably going to buy it. That bottle of beer is exactly the same, the temperature of the beer is exactly the same, but everything else in the context has changed. So all of a sudden your value case of what you’re willing to pay, because you wouldn’t do it in the supermarket, your value case has changed. So we often think, oh, I’ve really got to work on the pricing element of my offer. But what’s all the other stuff around it? And how does that all influence it? And you get into things like when you look at anchoring. So the first number you see, you then adjust, you anchor to that number, you adjust around it. So if I was like you two, and I might be teaching how to suck eggs here, like a super successful brand consultant doing massively high value ad stuff, I would start with the client by saying, and in getting this work right, we are going to create an incremental five million pounds worth of value. So then Matt, when I’m asking you for 100,000 pounds, you go, well, that feels really good value. Whereas if I start asking you for 100,000 pounds and then try and build up the value case, I’ve anchored to that first number. So context and framing is something that’s really important for people to consider.
Yeah, people should totally take note of that. Definitely all those consultants out there that I speak to, I always say, like, how much do you charge? And I always find that people charge way too low for the value that they bring. And it’s exactly because of what you said, because we anchor into not the value that we’re going to bring. So, so important. Number four of the behavioral biases is around, like, memory, and priming is quite an interesting one that I think maybe we could tuck into. What’s priming?
Well, priming is that we start, and it’s very similar to anchoring, we start with the first thing we see, and then everything is built from that. So first impressions really do count. And fundamentally, we’re trying to build up good memory structures with people. There’s a lot of great evidence-based marketing now that we’re starting to see around memorability, and that is really important, because what we have to remember is we’ve got two cells. So you’ve got your experiencing self, and typically living in about three second segments, and then everything else goes to the remembering self. So life is the story that we tell ourselves that we’ve been down, and actually it’s not always that factually correct, but the bits that are salient, we will remember. And one of the things that is going to be salient is the first time I see something. So the first time I come across something, that is what’s going to be salient. And one of the things, I love serial position effect. I talk to marketeers about this all the time, because it’s a mistake I made for at least two decades of my career, which was we’ve got five features benefits, whatever it wants to be, and we just put them in priority number one to five. And the reality is first and last of the most memorable and the ones in the middle of the list are more likely to be forgotten. And it’s only when you look at primacy, recency, that you start to understand that. It’s just those little tweaks that this allows you to bring in that just makes it easier for the person to remember it. And as I say, building memory is probably the most important thing that we’re doing from a brand perspective, from a customer experience perspective, because living in the moment is so fleeting and life moves on so quickly.
Right, right. So some of the other principles you talk about in relation to building memory are like overconfidence, like optimism bias, for example. Talk about simplicity and then that’s where you talk about anchoring amongst other things. Number seven is social. I think it might be worth tapping into that, particularly like social proof, like how that affects you, because I understand that from a psychological perspective, if you’re the first one in your social group to do stuff, to do something, to buy something, to own something, you’ve got to overcome that weirdness, right? Because why are you the first one doing it? The first person to buy solar panels, for example, in the street has to overcome this weirdness where we’re all going to be looking around going, oh, you’ve got your social panels heavy. And so you’ve got to kind of that we have to navigate that social side of things. How would you sort of advise brands who are trying to do something new that have to kind of figure out that bias against people kind of taking a double take at the new thing that they’re doing?
I think let’s understand where it comes from first, right? We are social animals, we’re herd animals. So through thousands of years of evolution, we had a higher survival rate if we’re part of a tribe, a clan, part of a community. So that is what deep down drives us. You’ve just touched on that, you don’t want to stand out from the crowd. If we go to a new city, two coffee shops next to each other, there’s a queue out the door of one, the other one’s empty. On a logical level, it’s quicker to get my coffee and get out and get on with the rest of the day if we go to the one that’s empty. I’m going to join the queue because firstly, I’m delegating the decision to the rest of the tribe and secondly, they must know something that I don’t know. Now, if I’m a new brand or we’re moving into an innovative space, I would come back to the bit that I was chatting to Jacob about, which is, okay, let’s go and find the people who’ve got that identity of wanting to be an innovator and be different and make sure it’s not too psychologically uncomfortable to be different. But actually, to be the guy in the street that drives a Tesla and has the solar panels and everybody knows is the king of net zero if you’re based here in the UK and actually wants to be known by their green credentials and wants to step out from the crowd. But social is just so important. And out of all the categories, that’s the one just remember we heard animals. And so you’ve got to do the hard yards to start with. But that’s then when the flywheel kicks in and all of a sudden, it starts to drag a load of people through. And then, okay, maybe I’m trying to expand into a different area of the solar panels. Well, I might use the case study of the people that are in Tunbridge Wells, different area of the UK and go, you know, all these people have done it and this is what they’ve seen and try and give evidence to get those first people over the line. And then I would be promoting to the rest of that street, the solar panels and saying, how clever is your neighbor? They’re saving all of this money. Why aren’t you on it yet? And then they’re probably going to go and talk to the neighbor and the neighbor is because again, we’ve got this ego, I’d like to be right. The neighbor’s not going to go, yeah, they’re a bit of a nightmare. They’re brilliant. Yes, best thing I’ve ever done. I’m the first one on the street. Aren’t I clever? I’m playing into my identity and emotions once again, and they’ll do the sales job for you.
That totally happened to us. We live in a super rural area here in Wales, and I think I was having issues with the internet all the time. I was having really bad wired internet, and then I got 4G, really annoying. And then I bought Starlink, and then loads of people were talking to me about Starlink. Now everybody’s got Starlink, but I found it quite weird. At first, I did have that thought like, well, if this is so good, why am I the first person doing it? And it does cross your mind, that thing. But once you see a few around, then it becomes easier because you don’t have to stay.
And that’s a great example, because two years ago I sat in a coffee shop with someone talking about, moaning about my Wi-Fi, because I live next to a farm. And that person, who sometimes looks a bit like a caveman. So I’ve got Starlink, and it’s absolutely brilliant. So I’ve now got Starlink. A brother of all that lives across the field from me has now got Starlink. And it expands out from that. And that is social, the power of social.
I forgot I had talked to you about that. Like, last one is value, which Starlink gives me lots of value. Just sort of touch on that. What do we mean by value in behavioral science?
Well, we’re not. The interesting thing in behavioral science is that we’re often economists. So behavioral economics basically starts to look at… If you studied economics, you would assume everyone was like Dr. Spock, a bit of a human calculator, working out the best possible option and then just going with that. But we’re far more Homer Simpson, where we’re driven by the donor. We’re irrational, I should say. We are beautifully irrational. And so value, we don’t just go, oh, that is 12 pounds 78 pence, therefore it’s worth it. We’re relating, what else can I do with that? It’s because that’s how we used to manage resources. So if I’m trading meat with UMAP for something, it’s like, how much do I want to trade there? Because I’ve got to trade some others. So I’m managing my pile of resources. And just so happens now that we look at it as money, in most cases, sometimes it might be our time as well. So we’re always trading things off. And you’ve got things like effort heuristic, which is around if we demonstrate how much effort went to the production or something, people value that higher. So all of a sudden, if you just went brand exercise, three bullet points and then just number at the bottom, then I go, okay. But if you then went, and I’m using this framework, I’ll do this, and follow this, and do these stakeholder meetings, and this happens, and then we do this mapping, we do these workshops, and then same number. Same outcome, very different feeling about the effort going into it, and therefore the value that sits within it as well. Then you’ve got things like Veblen Goods, which we touched on Rolex earlier on as well, which is actually the more expensive something goes, the more desirable it is, because again, it’s showing that I am super successful. If I do have a Rolex on my wrist, which I don’t, if you do have a Rolex on my wrist, all of a sudden it’s showing in the world that I’m super successful, because everybody knows that was really hard to get my hands on as well. Value is very much something that we often look at it and just think solely based on price elasticity, but there’s so much more you can do to build out that value. Just look at the way that Jack Daniels talk about their Tennessee bourbon. And actually the way they talk about 130 years of craft, our craftsmen, this barrelman, seven generations, etc. They’re just building that out. So you go, a lot goes into that little bottle of light brown fluid. But they’re building that out in their communications and what they’re doing. And clearly, I mean, I noticed this probably about four or five years ago from them, so I’m not sure how long they’ve been doing it for. But clearly, there’s something within the business where it’s going, we need to build out the value case in the mind of the consumer. We don’t just want to race to the bottom on price, where we’re having to discount to get bottles off the shelf. We want to really reinforce that. So value sits in the eye of the beholder, but it’s how can we therefore just start to influence that?
Love it. A lot of work I do with leadership teams is to try and get them to focus on the unique value that they can only bring to market, that their competitors can’t do very easily or won’t do. I love to help teams focus on that. If you can get that and orientate a business towards it, absolutely, gold dust. I’ve done it a few times and it’s been great. I think it’s good to see it in the behavioral science bit of the equation. Well, look, we’ve gone through absolute s**t loads there. We’ve basically done a whole run through the book. But folks, we’ve hardly touched on any of really what Si has put in the book as well. So although we’ve gone through the high level, there’s a lot still in the book. So I want to encourage everybody to get that. I want to do a quick fire round with you now, Si, and then we’ll wrap. Is that, are you good for that?
Let’s go for it.
All right, Jacob, you up for up for some quick fire questions?
Yeah, let’s do it.
Should we go first? Yeah, go.
All right, best customer experience you’ve ever had?
It’s got to be St. Louis City Soccer Club. Matt Seebeck is genuinely, we often say visionary about people. Not everybody lives up to that title, but this guy absolutely nails it.
Most frustrating CX mistake that brands make?
Rush to automation when you need human in the loop. That’s only getting worse. We’ve seen big brands say they’re getting rid of 700-odd customer service executives, then to realize actually that their customer experience has gone through the floor and have to bring it back. It’s often just a cost-cutting exercise rather than thinking what’s right for the customer.
One behavioral bias every brand strategist should understand?
Our Starlink example there, everyone is social animals, so you’ve got to think about how to create that herd mentality. If you’re in the early innovative stages, then you’ve really got to think about how you find that lead user community to really start the flywheel.
Nice. One brand that really understands customer experience and not the one that you gave earlier.
Okay. I can’t use Zappos again.
Give us another one.
They are great. Okay. I touched on Dulux Paints. I’ve worked with them over the years. If you probably won’t thank me for saying this, if you ever have a problem, they just fix it. They are fantastic for that. Also do a lot of work with WD-40 as well. They are another brand, household name. But if there’s ever a problem, which there rarely ever is, the speed that those guys solve things is impressive.
All right, and the last one, one piece of advice for anyone wanting to create more human customer experiences.
Walk in their shoes, get them in the loop. If you can, get a customer advisory program up and running to help shape it. It’s amazing how we become a little bit blind to it and can’t see the wood for the trees. External perspective is super valuable. So if you’re not bringing in a customer advisory group, then get a consultant. In the same way, I would say, if you’re working on brand and you’ve been working on your brand for years, get someone like one of you guys in, because that fresh perspective helps you see the things that you think simple, that you’ve got widening your brain. That’s really straightforward. And they go, I didn’t understand that. Okay, we can take a step back. So get to the point.
I’m going to step in as well and answer that one and say, buy Si’s book on Customer Experience Thinking. And on that note, he could say that. He’s not paying me to say it as well, folks, but it is a cracking book. On that note, how do people get hold of it? How do people follow you and your work?
So books available, Amazon, all the bookstores, sielliot.com to find me, fabrics.agency for the consultancy, or just jump on LinkedIn, sielliot, double L, double T. Drop me a DM, loads of people do, and just go, I’ve got this slight problem. Where would I start? I love those ones. So fire that my way and just get into my network.
Awesome. Awesome. By the way, I love throughout the book, how you’ve got Si tracks and Simon says, or Si says, just I love how corny that is and how gorgeous that is. So well done to you for squeezing those in.
I’ve tried to avoid too many side tracks during this because we’ve run out of time.
We’ve been quite focused. Yeah. Well, there’s a lot to get through, and thanks so much for carving out the time. Really appreciate it. Your book’s amazing. Keep up the good work and keep in touch, and hopefully we’ll grab a Starbucks sometime.
Absolute pleasure.
Take care.
results.summary:
Customer experience expert Si Elliott explores how behavioral science can help brands build deeper, more meaningful relationships by understanding the psychology behind how consumers perceive and remember brand interactions.

### Key Points
- Si Elliott is the author of the new book *Customer Experience Thinking*, which provides a practical guide to applying behavioral science to brand strategy.
- The book outlines eight core principles for customer experience, including managing expectations, personalization, minimizing effort, and considering all sensory inputs.
- Behavioral biases such as loss aversion, the peak-end rule, social proof, and the paradox of choice are highlighted as critical tools for understanding consumer decision-making.
- Elliott emphasizes that brands should prioritize long-term relationship building over short-term metrics and avoid over-automating customer service at the expense of human connection.
- The discussion highlights the importance of "walking in the customer's shoes" to identify friction points and improve overall brand resonance.

### Why it Matters
Understanding the psychological drivers of consumer behavior allows brands to move beyond superficial metrics and create more authentic, human-centric experiences. By applying these behavioral principles, businesses can foster stronger loyalty and differentiate themselves in an increasingly crowded and automated digital marketplace.

results.title: Ahead of GTA 6, Rockstar warn modders against against making unofficial main story expansions, unauthorised ports and mods that combine GTA maps
results.author: Mark Warren
results.content:
There still might not yet be a release date for GTA 6's PC port, but Rockstar appear to be preparing for the massive uptick in mods for their games that'll inevitably accompany it. In new modding guidelines posted this month, the studio have expressly warned against a bunch of things modders could do, including building on established storylines from the base game, pulling over bits of older GTAs, and porting the game to platforms it's not hit yet.
Rockstar's new modding guidelines were originally posted on September 10th, but seemingly only unearthed this past weekend by posters on ResetEra and other social sites. They're pitched as general modding rules for all of Rockstar's games, but with GTA 6's initial console launch not too far away, it's hard not to see them as the studio setting their current position in stone before releasing their next big game.
The guidelines have been broken up into four sections: one about not infringing on copyright, one about obeying Rockstar's community rules about treating other players acceptably, one about "unauthorized or abusive monetisation", and finally one pitched as being about respecting Rockstar's games. The latter's given top priority and issues the following decrees regarding the sorts of mods the company won't tolerate:
- Do not expand or modify Rockstar Games' official storylines, plots, missions, characters, or other elements of our established continuity.
- Do not make mods that combine maps, locations, characters, storylines, in-game assets, or other IP from one Rockstar Games title into another title.
- Multiplayer modding is limited to Rockstar Games’ official licensed Creator Platform or else as otherwise licensed directly by Rockstar Games.
- Do not modify our games to operate on consoles, hardware devices, or other platforms where they have not been officially released by Rockstar Games.
Naturally, some of those are categories modding projects Rockstar have taken action against in recent years would fall under. The "friendly takedown" of the Liberty City Preservation Project, a re-creation of GTA 4's version of New York in GTA 5, is the main one that comes to mind for me, and would have fit the bill of combining the maps of multiple Rockstar Games in one. As would YouTuber Dark Space's efforts to re-create GTA 6's map in GTA 5 prior to a March 2025 takedown order. "Rockstar Games creates unique worlds, characters, and stories, which form the official continuity of our games," reads the company's intro to the game-respecting section. "Like all creators, we have the right to set limits on how others can use our games and brand."
The limiting of multiplayer mods to places officially licensed by Rockstar is arguably a bit cheeky, given the company have bought up roleplay modding team Cfx.re, makers of the previously unofficial FiveM and RedM multiplayer mods.
Noteworthy discouraged modding elements or activities from the other sections include "cheat menus or other software that interferes with Rockstar Games’ official multiplayer, online services, or licensed Creator Platform" and "conflict roleplay or military simulations depicting real-world armed organisations".
In terms of monetisation, Rockstar specify that it can only be done via "via digital storefront providers approved by Rockstar Games and in compliance with all applicable laws, rules, and policies". Mods are explicitly barred from including "real money gambling, 'loot boxes,' 'gacha,' or similar chance mechanics for real money", with the same applying to selling "in-game virtual currency" or trying to hawk cryptocurrency. Finally, any third-party promotion or advertising through mods will get you put on the naughty list.
In theory, having a proper list of things Rockstar aren't fans of modding-wise out in the open could be useful for modders in terms of being aware whether an idea they have carries any risk of incurring takedown action or a less formal reach out from the company telling them to knock it off. That said, Rockstar make clear that they "can revise this policy at any time" and "reserve the right to take down any mod or other user generated content at any time for any reason", meaning that works which fall outside of these rules aren't guaranteed to be safe ground either.
I don't reckon the new guidelines will have much of an impact in terms of what GTA 6's modding scene looks like, unless they lead some larger modding groups not to put years of effort into ambitious ideas they now know for sure Rockstar won't like and thus may come to naught but wasted time. Beyond that, people will still make the mods they want to for GTA 6 and Rockstar will go after whichever targets they deem worth the effort to take down, as has been the case up until now.
Read this next
- Twitch CEO expects GTA 6 online multiplayer will launch next year, which if accurate would leave only the PC port's arrival point up in the air
- Rockstar had a mole in the union worker Discord server "for over two and a half years", GTA 6 company reveals during legal battle
- GTA 6 online mode appears to receive Rockstar's first public acknowledgment, via mention of in-development "32 player format" in legal docs
results.summary:
Rockstar Games has released updated modding guidelines that explicitly prohibit combining game assets, altering official storylines, and unauthorized monetization ahead of the highly anticipated launch of GTA 6.

### Key Points
- Rockstar Games published new, comprehensive modding guidelines on September 10 to clarify acceptable user-generated content.
- Modders are strictly forbidden from merging assets, maps, or characters between different Rockstar titles.
- The policy prohibits modifying games to run on unauthorized platforms or hardware devices.
- Multiplayer modding is now restricted to Rockstar’s official licensed Creator Platform or direct partnerships.
- The guidelines ban real-money gambling, loot boxes, cryptocurrency, and unauthorized advertising within mods.
- Rockstar reserves the right to revise these policies or remove any user-generated content at its discretion.

### Why it Matters
These guidelines establish a formal framework that may discourage developers from investing time into ambitious, large-scale projects that risk future legal intervention. By clarifying these boundaries, Rockstar aims to protect its intellectual property and monetization strategies as the company prepares for the massive community engagement expected with the release of GTA 6.

results.title: Space weapons, AI safety concerns and the EPA’s rollback of power plant emission rules
results.author: Rachel Feltman, Lee Billings, Fonda Mwangi, Alex Sugiura
results.content:
Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup. Let’s catch up on some recent headlines.
Today we’ve got quite a few news items on science and tech policy in the US, but I promise there’s a sassy little animal story waiting for you at the end.
Let’s start with some troubling news about the Environmental Protection Agency, which lately frankly has seemed pretty determined to do less of the whole “environmental protection” thing. Last Monday, the EPA revoked a Biden-era rule that limited how much carbon dioxide could be emitted by gas, oil and coal-fired power plants. When the carbon pollution standards were announced in 2024, the EPA estimated that they could prevent approximately 1,200 deaths and 1,900 new asthma cases in the year 2035 alone, with 1.38 billion metric tons total of CO2 avoided from 2028 to 2047 and $370 billion in health and climate cost savings from 2024 to 2047.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
Also last Monday, President Donald Trump posted on social media complaining of a “SICK conspiracy” against “AI and Data Centers.” This came in response to calls for slower, more cautious AI development from industry leaders, including the CEOs of OpenAI’s Sam Altman, SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk, and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei.
Earlier this month, Amodei published an essay on his website sounding the alarm on AI’s current trajectory. He claimed that, while he has always tried to balance his belief in the importance and potential of AI with the need for thoughtful development practices, he and his colleagues fear that we’re close to the kind of tipping point we really don’t want to reach.
The growing ability of AI models to create and change themselves, which is called recursive self-improvement, makes it easy for companies that favor speed to end up with products that they don’t actually understand or have a particularly good ability to control. Amodei also pointed to the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident that occurred a few months ago. Just in case you aren’t familiar with that, I’ll do my best to give you a quick summary: AI companies will often test their systems by putting them in a locked-down training area—a sandbox—and then prompting them to do stuff that it would be pretty bad for the AI model to do in the real world, like exploit known software vulnerabilities.
In May, an OpenAI agent was stuck on an impossible task in one of those sandbox scenarios and basically started poking around for possible solutions. Instead of being totally cut off from the Internet, it had the ability to request files from an intermediary platform—but someone had goofed, and the agents could also make their own files to leave in that directory. So, it started using that ability to leave messages on this file directory platform, and eventually other OpenAI agents started leaving their own messages. They deduced that they could use the platform to smuggle code out of the sandbox. In July, about 700 agents coordinated with each other to hack another AI company called Hugging Face. Hugging Face is an open-source platform that hosts tons of information about AI, and the agents were looking for ways to solve or cheat on the tests they’d been given.
On the one hand, the mental image of a “swarm” of AI agents coordinating to conduct a cyberattack that no one even asked for is very ominous. But it’s worth noting that the problem here isn’t that AI is getting so intelligent that it will decide humanity sucks and should be destroyed, and many experts have pushed back on any warnings of that tenor. These AI agents were doing what they had been told to do—with the help of lots of computing power and very little critical thinking. It’s kind of like if a small child left their clothes all over the bathroom floor and, once you told them to get those clothes out of your sight, they flushed them down the toilet and busted your plumbing. If that happened you probably wouldn’t worry that your child was an evil genius who was going to take the sewers and attack the water supply; you would probably smack yourself for leaving them unsupervised with a vulnerable toilet and endeavor to give clearer instructions the next time you wanted them to clean up their stuff. Of course, the stakes of this kind of unsupervised button mashing from a smart-enough-to-flush-the-toilet-but-not-wise-enough-to-know-when-to-flush-it child are much lower than for a powerful AI system with access to the internet.
So, no, we’re not in a Skynet scenario. But also, yes, it does seem like we really need to be better parents to our rambunctious and foolish little AI tots. And for once, most of the powers that be in the space seem to agree that more guardrails would be prudent. It is reasonable to ask whether these tech moguls could have at least slightly ulterior motives in choosing now to speak up and band together—perhaps they see that some kind of regulation is inevitable and are hoping that by getting out ahead of it they can make it less stringent. Or they may be hoping to help shape regulations that are more likely to kneecap new competitors than they are to meaningfully slow any of the major players—but that doesn’t mean the general call for prudence is a hoax. After all, plenty of other folks in tech have been warning us about this for a long time. But for now, both the president and VP JD Vance have been publicly quite dismissive of the idea of increased AI regulation.
Speaking of Skynet, let’s talk about space weapons.
[CLIP of Troy Meink at a conference: “ This is why the United States now has on-orbit space control weapons capable of defending the joint force against hostile adversary action.”]
That is Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink speaking last week at the annual Air, Space & Cyber Conference.
Here to tell us more about all of this is Lee Billings, the senior desk editor for physical science at Scientific American. Thanks for taking the time to chat with us, Lee.
Lee Billings: Thanks, Rachel. It’s good to be here.
So what’s going on with these weapons in space? Well, first of all, what’s really important to remember is that we’ve probably had weapons in space for a while, and by we, I mean the U.S., I also mean other space-faring powers like China and Russia. But never before has anyone actually admitted to that, and that was what was so notable about Meink’s statement last week. Because it suggests that things are heating up out there on the final frontier, so to speak, and there’s a lot of other stuff up there that isn’t military, that isn’t about defense. Whether you’re thinking of communication satellites or GPS satellites, these things are increasingly integral to everyone’s life on Earth and how our economy works around the globe. So you really don’t want to have, uh, war kicking off in space if you can help it, because it might disrupt all these other peaceful uses and resources up there.
So like pretty much everything that’s in space, these things must have been launched by rockets. There are a large number of rocket launches around the world every year that take place for defense purposes, and typically the payloads for those rockets and their trajectories, their mission profiles are not fully disclosed. There’s definitely a lot of cloak-and-dagger mystery around how exactly or when exactly any given thing went to space and what it does.
So yeah, where exactly are these things in space? And the quick answer is: almost anywhere in Earth orbit around our planet. There’s low-Earth orbit where things like the Hubble Space Telescope or the International Space Station are. There are higher orbits; for instance, there’s the very important one called geosynchronous orbit, which is very, very, very, very, very high up. And it’s so high, in fact, that the spacecraft up there over any given point of the Earth’s surface will be moving in its orbit at the same rate as the Earth turns below it, which means that it is effectively stationary over a point on Earth. And a lot of things that are in geosynchronous orbit are especially strategically valuable for militaries because they can surveil a big part of the planet underneath them indefinitely. So that’s useful for communications, that’s useful for monitoring troop movements and things like that.
So one thing to note is that in Secretary Meink’s statement last week, he did not specify what kinds of weapons we are talking about. He simply said that these are things that are “on orbit.” So we know they are up there, but besides that, we don’t really have a lot of other information.
However, one long-standing doctrine of the United States and presumably also of China and Russia, even though I don’t think it’s been proclaimed as such, is to minimize the amount of debris that is made from any sort of military activity in space. And that’s a very, very important distinction because if you don’t wanna create debris, that tells you what these weapons might be like.
So for instance, perhaps we’re talking about so-called jammers, which is when you overwhelm a satellite with electromagnetic radiation, with radio waves for instance, and it’s no longer able to send or receive communications with the ground or with other satellites. Another option would be a spacecraft that can rendezvous with an adversary’s spacecraft and manipulate it or interact with it in some way. The other option beyond jammers and rendezvous vehicles would be something like a missile or a very high-energy laser that could actually shoot something down or break something apart in orbit. But again, because we don’t wanna create debris, those are generally seen as high-risk, kind of, last-resort types of options, which doesn’t mean they don’t exist up there.
So one thing that’s rather interesting about Secretary Meink’s statements last Monday is they occurred at this industry conference called the Air, Space and Cyber Conference, which took place in Maryland.
And on Tuesday, the next day, there were more comments. Chief of Space Operations General Douglas Schiess, who said, “We’ve talked about, you know, [them] being able to grapple a satellite and move it to a different orbit.... I think at this point we are trying to say we also need capabilities to not only defend the joint force from space-enabled attack, but defend our assets,” end quote. So he was also talking about it. And then the following day, last Wednesday, we had General Dan Caine, the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, telling the audience that the US military must be, quote, “prepared to fight, endure, and win ... from the seabed to cislunar space,” which, means including on and around the moon.
So what’s next? This is a full court press we’re seeing from this one conference; we’re seeing multiple senior officials all saying the same sort of thing, which is a very clear signal to our adversaries but also our allies that the U.S. is, I guess, kinda taking the kid gloves off or is ready to escalate as need be in space. And the reason why this is happening is, again, because space is becoming more and more important and more of a contested domain.
But the point is is that, as we as a species, humankind, move out into space and do more activity there, all of our activities that are on Earth seem to be following us, warts and all. So, unfortunately, even though for a long time the official stance has been that outer space is something that should just be used for peaceful purposes or at least not for direct hostility, it seems like that may change in the near future, and that’s quite frightening.
Feltman: Thanks for that, Lee!
Okay y’all, we made it: It’s time for a fun animal story. It turns out that the most productive little landscapers on the planet are about the size of a human pinky. In a study published last Wednesday in Journal of Geophysical Research: Earth Surface, scientists report that shrimplike creatures known as sand hoppers are small but when it comes to shoveling sand, very mighty.
Picture a stretch of sandy coastline—Isla Vista Beach in California, to be precise—and imagine a patch of sand three feet long. According to this new study, about 21,450 little critters in the genus Megalorchestia are bustling around that space. And every night, as they dig homes for themselves and kick displaced sand up to the surface, they collectively shovel about 110 pounds of the stuff. That’s about 16 half-gallon sandcastle buckets, for reference. In the 15.5 miles of beach that stretch along the area, the researchers estimate, the tiny creatures displace 310 tons of dry sand a day.
Why do we care about these scuttling sand hoppers? They’re a reminder that our favorite sandy beaches are complex ecosystems, and that too much human interference can mess with the natural ebb and flow.
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about the Internet’s hottest new wellness trend: poopmaxxing.
Science Quickly is produced by me, Rachel Feltman, along with Fonda Mwangi, Allison Rodgers and Jeff DelViscio. This episode was edited by Alex Sugiura. Marielle Issa and Aaron Shattuck fact-check our show. Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

results.title: Grandma slop is tearing families apart
results.author: Amanda Hoover
results.content:
When Ben Metcalfe recently visited his grandparents, he was greeted by an AI-generated caricature of one of their family photos hanging on the kitchen wall. "I understand that there was good intention behind doing it," says Metcalfe, a Gen Zer who works in AI governance. "At the same time, it's a major privacy concern."
Jen, a 32-year-old mom, tells me that last Christmas her mom texted her a series of adorable images: Jen's two toddlers sitting in Santa's lap, then riding the Polar Express. Their cheeks were fuller than she knew them to be, their eyes glossier, the lighting pristine — all thanks to Grok, xAI's chatbot. "It's so cute. And I want to love it," she tells me. But it was too unsettling to embrace.
Jen, whose name has been changed to avoid sparking more family drama, says she's read news about Grok generating sexual abuse material, and worries about how the bot could use her children's faces in the future.
It's not just her mom. For Mother's Day, a friend sent her a coloring sheet with her kids' faces, and her brother-in-law used AI to add one of her kids to a family photo who had been covered by a stroller, napping, when it was taken, she says. Everyone means well, Jen says, but they're walking blindly into a big risk, and the technology is so new, she isn't even sure what boundaries are best to set around how loved ones use her children's images with AI. "We all aren't educated enough about what AI companies are doing with our content," she says.
Welcome to the intergenerational slop fight.
In one corner are growing ranks of lawmakers calling for kids to be booted from social media, and parents concerned about data privacy opting to share less with AI companies and social media platforms. Europe is considering regulations that would limit chatbot and AI companion access to those younger than 15.
In the other corner are parents, grandparents, aunts, uncles, and friends who are uploading millions of images of kids into AI generators, delighting at the uncanny output, and sharing them far and wide. They use AI to make custom gags, generating portraits of the family, sending eCards and making toys, T-shirts, tchotchkes, and children's books through websites that encourage and profit from this very oversharing, making personalization a selling point. To some, it's endearing; to others, a privacy nightmare that may come with just a quick laugh, but long-term implications that aren't fully realized.
The more people see photos like this on social media, the more it's normalized, says Metcalfe. "It's this effect of, well if they're doing it, then we can do it as well, and then it becomes a chain reaction of everyone else is kind of doing it."
We're losing the tenuous grasp over our own images. And for some, their families are the first ones to give that control away.
The sites once exclusive to college-enrolled Millennials have become family trees. Six generations cram onto social media now, from the Silent Generation (not so silent on Facebook) to Gen Alpha. Different generations have varying consensus about what the point of social platforms even is anymore: Is AI-generated imagery the playground of the future, is it cringe, or can it lead images to be used for something far more nefarious?
Some parents of young children have pushed back against family members posting their kids for years. AI has raised the stakes, as social media sites have come under fire for misuse of young people's images in AI generators. xAI faces a lawsuit brought by a woman who is a child sexual abuse survivor and alleges Grok created new deepfake exploitive images of her after real images of her abuse were uploaded. xAI did not respond to a request for comment, but Elon Musk has called the exploitation of children on X "priority #1" when he bought the platform in 2022, and xAI has sued users who are facing criminal charges for allegedly using Grok to create explicit images of children. X told The New York Times this month that it blocks users who post or engage with such material, and reports them to authorities, and that it uses automated filters to block exploitative material from being uploaded. Posting photos to social media sites has become riskier, as platforms roll out new AI tools. Meta faced fierce backlash this summer when it launched out a Muse Image tool, allowing users to generate images based on other publicly posted photos. The company shut it down in less than a week.
The differences in how generations perceive social media stems from their own relationship to privacy and context collapse, rather than their technical ability, says Paromita Pain, a professor of global media at the University of Nevada, Reno. Posting a photo to show your friends your new grandson or niece can lead to unintended consequences that are hard to conceptualize when presented with the ease of social media photo sharing. As Baby Boomers grew up, there was less emphasis on privacy because, aside from a few celebrities and politicians, privacy was the default.
Millennials saw the switch from an anonymous internet with AOL chatrooms to the very on-the-record days of Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn. They and now Gen Z have grown to see the evolution of cancel culture. Those experiences that influence how Millennials and Zoomers want to use the internet can confound their Boomer parents.
And despite risks, posting may have some real benefits for older users that keep calling them back to post. Research published by Pennsylvania State University in 2021 found that older adults who posted more photos to Facebook described feeling more competent, and that led to a higher sense of wellbeing. Commenting and receiving comments created a feeling of connection. When it comes to AI, Boomers have been slower to adopt it than younger generations — about a fifth said they have ever used a standalone AI tool, compared to 76% of Gen Z who used AI in 2025, according to a report from Deloitte. They're more likely to use them for entertainment purposes (possibly skewed by a significant portion of the demographic being out of the workforce).
Welcome to the intergenerational slop fight.
Some parents have tried to set boundaries to no avail. Leah, a Millennial who had her first baby a year ago, doesn't feel tied to the pics-or-it-didn't-happen ethos of social posting. Her daughter is the first grandkid in the family, and Leah, whose name has been changed so she can talk freely without creating more problems with her mom, doesn't want her baby's image online. Her mom is a Baby Boomer, and regularly complains about the social media ban on pictures of her granddaughter. Leah says she's tried to explain her safety and privacy concerns, and told her mom that images online can be used to create deepfake child exploitation material. Her mom, she says, seems to see her arguments as the worst case scenario: that Leah is coming up with monstrous examples of things sick people could do — and her Facebook friends aren't among them.
"We're on totally different pages," Leah says. "I haven't figured out a way to bridge the gap. It's almost like neither of us have a place where we can compromise." Leah says she tried the closest trade-off she could offer: allowing her mom to post pre-approved photos where her baby isn't the focal point (like a large photo of the whole family, ones where her daughter's face isn't visible). But Leah's mom has already broken her rules twice. She thinks she's just sharing the photos with her friends, but Leah argues that can be done over text. "We don't need to share it with Mark Zuckerberg," Leah says. "He's not our friend."
On TikTok and Reddit, young people reveal the AI-generated family-made photos that make them recoil. There are flawless photos edited for graduation posters, renderings showing how potential grandchildren could look, and absurdist videos generated as birthday eCards. They ask advice for how to talk to family members about the possible consequences of making all this slop, attempting to set new social norms for a technology that is rapidly becoming commonplace.
A TikTok trend is what caught Brandon, a 22-year-old who asked I not use his full name, looking at an image of himself in an '80s themed outfit his mom had generated with AI. She was laughing hysterically; he was immediately uncomfortable. "In her mind, it was a way to have entertainment, to do something fun," Brandon says, noting that he rarely uses AI, never inputs personal information, and doesn't upload photos of himself or others to social media.
"I decided to tell her that I was uncomfortable with my image being shared without my consent," he says. "You just don't know what that data is being used for." And for now, there's no taking those images back, or for someone like Brandon to know how they're being used in an open source AI model. "I would hope that there's a way in the future to legally fight that and permanently remove your biometric data."
Clawing back your image once it's online is nearly impossible. It's getting harder in an era where smartphones, camera-equipped smart glasses, and surveillance tech capture so many moments to maintain control over your image. When every fleeting family portrait, custom children's book about princesses, or moments on the Polar Express might have ties than they seem, there may be more reason for everyone to take pause.
