results.title: The ECB will invest in tokenised securities, and settle the trades on its own new rail
results.author: Ana-Maria Stanciuc
results.content:
The European Central Bank is preparing to put some of its own money into tokenized securities, moving from building the plumbing for digital asset markets to buying in them.
Settlement will occur in central bank money, routed through Pontes, the system the Eurosystem has built for trades running on distributed ledger technology.
What the bank intends to buy is conventional enough in substance: euro-denominated debt issued by central and regional governments in the euro area, by their agencies, and by European supranational bodies. Only the wrapper is new.
The announcement commits the bank to a “small portion” of the portfolio without attaching a figure, and leaves the operational details and timing to the Executive Board until that groundwork is done.
That decision is to take account of how tokenized issuance actually develops, which is a way of saying the size of the program depends on how much there turns out to be to buy.
The money is coming from the ECB’s own funds portfolio. That is not a monetary policy instrument: it is the pot whose returns help pay the bank’s running costs, with supervision funded separately.
So the institution is risking its own income rather than conducting an operation on the euro area economy, which is a smaller thing than it might sound and also the reason it can move at all.
Rather than watching tokenized markets from the regulator’s chair, the bank wants to work through an entire investment cycle itself, from executing a trade to settling it to running the systems and managing the position afterward. Institutions that only supervise a market tend to learn about it late.
Pontes is one of the two strands the ECB named; the other is Appia, which is meant to produce a blueprint for tokenized finance across Europe.
Together they are the bank’s answer to the question of how central bank money keeps working in markets that increasingly settle on ledgers, or, in the announcement’s phrase, how to keep it “fit for the digital age”.
This is separate from the retail digital euro, which is a consumer payment instrument rather than a wholesale settlement rail, and which the ECB is developing on its own timetable.
What the bank has not said is which securities, in what quantity, or on what date.

The European Central Bank plans to invest its own funds into tokenized securities to gain practical experience with distributed ledger technology and modern wholesale settlement systems.

### Key Points
- The ECB will purchase euro-denominated debt issued by regional governments, agencies, and European supranational bodies.
- Trades will be settled using central bank money via the Eurosystem’s proprietary Pontes distributed ledger platform.
- The initiative uses the bank’s own funds portfolio rather than monetary policy instruments, meaning it does not directly impact the broader euro area economy.

- This project is distinct from the retail digital euro, which remains a separate development focused on consumer payment instruments.

### Why it Matters
By actively participating in tokenized markets, the ECB aims to ensure that central bank money remains a viable settlement asset in an increasingly digitized financial landscape. This hands-on approach allows the institution to gain technical expertise and regulatory foresight that would be impossible to achieve solely through external supervision.

results.title: I Tried Two Extraordinary Security Gadgets Made for Spots Other Tech Can’t Reach
results.author: Tyler Lacoma
results.content:
Abode Security Sensors 2026
Pros & Cons
- Accurate and speedy sensors for areas other security sensors aren't made for
- Tests showed excellent performance on garage door and fence gate
- Abode's hub automatically connects to sensors and makes setup one of the easiest I've done
- Offers a variety of automations and alert options through Abode's intuitive app
- Sensors have many additional applications for sheds, tilting windows and more
- Abode's standard hub requires a permanet Ethernet connection
- The outdoor contact sensor design could use another pass
A new crop of security sensors has hit the shelves in 2026, and I like what I’ve tested. Tiny sensors that can detect tampering, tilting, movement and so on are offering all-new ways to watch over specific parts of our home. Abode is the first security kit company I’ve seen embrace this tech by offering its first entirely new sensors in years, made for parts of the home that security systems don’t usually watch.
Abode has two new products available now, a sensor made to monitor garage door access ($35), and an outdoor access sensor ($50) designed for gates, sheds, barns and any door open to the elements. I got to try them both around my home, and found them particularly effective and easy to set up compared to many of the sensors I’ve tested.
If you’ve been looking for a special device to help monitor access to backyards, detached buildings on your property, or garage doors that always seem to get left open, these sensors are a remarkable answer, particularly if you already have an Abode system. If not, I’ll cover what you need to know from my testing.
Unboxing and setup
I was able to fully test an Abode starter security kit as well as its two new sensors for this review, providing a clear look at how the security brand functions. As far as setup experiences go, this has been one of my speediest. And I’ve tested many different systems.
Abode’s beginner’s kit is small, offering an indoor sensor, motion sensor and fob, along with the hub. I was pleased to find out, after downloading the app and connecting the hub, the other base devices automatically added themselves and made the setup process effortless, smoother than nearly any other security system except possibly Ikea’s affordable sensors.
Adding the new garage and outdoor sensors also proved quick, with pairing happening only seconds after I installed the batteries and typed in the activation code.
The one problem I have with Abode’s system is how the standard hub connects to Wi-Fi. This hub requires an Ethernet connection to your router or gateway, not only during setup but all the time. That’s a not-so-small problem if, like me, you have a router, gateway and other necessary devices already taking up all nearby outlets, which forced me to jury-rig a solution for the hub while I was testing.
Abode’s Iota hub does offer Wi-Fi, but that requires a more expensive upgrade to a $200 starter kit, not including extra sensors. It’s baffling that Abode’s standard hub still doesn’t support Wi-Fi when every other brand does. Check the outlets near your router before you choose this solution.
Garage sensor installation and performance
Equipped with internal gyroscope technology, Abode’s garage door sensor is made to detect orientation, and setup couldn’t be simpler. Using the included adhesive strips, I slapped the small monitor on my closed garage door, and it began accurately detecting open/closed states immediately in the Abode app.
Smart garage door motors and controllers can also do something like this, plus app controls, but this is one of the first standard home security systems to expand to the garage, and adding a single $50 sensor is far more affordable than replacing your garage controller entirely. Abode let me know if the garage was left open, and advised me on unexpected garage door movement when no one was at home, just as advertised.
Placing the sensor shouldn’t be any trouble, no matter what kind of garage you have. It sticks onto the inside of the garage door where there is plenty of space, and doesn’t require any complicated calibration. You may have to reset the sensor after placement to make sure it’s reading open and closed states correctly, but that, too, takes only moments.
Finally, you could use this sensor on anything that tilts up and down like a garage door, such as tilting windows, so it could have other applications in your home.
Gate sensor installation and performance
Abode’s outdoor access sensor proved more complicated than the garage monitor. Bulkier than most access sensors and equipped with weather-resistance capabilities, it’s made to tell when anything outdoors opens and shuts. The two parts sense when they are close or when they’ve moved apart, with a bit of extra leeway compared to indoor sensors, since outdoor fences and other access zones have varied designs and gaps.
The complex housing proved adequate, but was more frustrating to install and is in need of some future refinements. The screw-in backplate, for example, had pop-out sections to make room for the screws, but the plastic base was so thick I couldn’t put out the sections at all, not even with a hammer that nearly destroyed the base itself (I used another tool to carve them out eventually, not an ideal situation). And the battery casing was so tight and awkwardly designed, I was afraid forcing the batteries in would harm the nearby, unprotected circuitry.
In these ways, the design feels a little too close to a prototype model for me, and it probably needs another pass or two. But it works, and works very well, when it’s finally set up.
Connected to my old fence gate, the sensor accurately and immediately told me whenever it was opened or closed. I’ve found that gate left open more than a few times, so this gave me welcome peace of mind. I also tested it during a stormy downpour, which did nothing to affect the performance of the sensor.
You may want to turn off beeps from the hub that sound every time it alerts to the sensor being opened, but Abode provided a setting to do just that. However, alerts and monitoring aren’t the only things these sensors can do.
App automations that benefit from Abode’s support
One of the most impressive parts of Abode’s security platform is how it maintains connections to other third-party smart home gadgets, from Google Home connections to the rare-to-find Apple support for certain devices. There are also Abode’s own devices, including cameras and smart locks, which naturally work with the system
When Abode’s system is armed, triggering one of these garage or gate sensors can trip the system and sound a siren. But using the CUE automation tool in the Abode app, I found you can also set up many other types of automations, depending on what you want to activate.
This can include setting lights to turn on a warning glow if a fence gate is left open, or automatically unlocking your door when the garage is opened. You can also set times for these triggers to work, so they only function in the evening, on weekdays or only trigger after a certain time (the gate has been left open for 2 hours, for example). This adds more possibilities if you want to expand your smart home, but it’s not necessary to get value out of these sensors.
If you want to pay for an Abode subscription, you can add more features with plans starting at $80 a year, but these are mostly camera-focused, and I don’t think they’re necessary for these sensors at all.
Final thoughts on Abode’s new access sensors
Abode’s newest sensors offer exceptional performance in spots other sensors aren’t really made for. They’re also more expensive than typical sensors, and the outdoor sensor might need another design pass in the future, but I otherwise found them easy to set up and start using for customized, helpful alerts.
One word of caution: Abode’s standard hub requires an Ethernet connection, so consider where you’ll put it, and if you’ll need to run Ethernet cable anywhere during installation. Otherwise, this system sets itself up in minutes.
I’m enjoying this 2026 wave of security tech innovations. They’re finding new applications in the home – and finding them with success. Aqara’s multipurpose sensor is one such model. Abode’s proved another strong example, so if you’ve been looking for extended security capabilities outdoors or in the garage, take note of this update.

Abode has launched two specialized security sensors for 2026, designed to monitor garage doors and outdoor gates, offering homeowners expanded protection for areas typically ignored by standard security systems.

### Key Points
- The $35 garage door sensor uses internal gyroscope technology to detect tilt and orientation for accurate open/closed status monitoring.
- The $50 outdoor access sensor features weather-resistant housing designed for gates, sheds, and barns, though its physical installation process is currently cumbersome.
- Abode’s hub enables automatic device pairing and integrates with the CUE automation app to trigger lights, locks, or sirens based on sensor activity.
- The standard Abode hub requires a permanent Ethernet connection to a router, which may limit placement options for some users.
- Both sensors are compatible with existing Abode security kits and support third-party smart home ecosystems, including Google Home and Apple devices.

### Why it Matters
These sensors provide a cost-effective way to secure detached structures and garage entry points without requiring expensive smart-motor replacements or complex custom installations. By integrating these niche monitoring tools into a unified app, Abode allows users to create sophisticated home automations that improve both security and convenience.

results.title: iFixit Shares iPhone 18 Pro Teardown With Inside Look at New Features
results.author: Joe Rossignol
results.content:
iFixit today published an iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max teardown in both article and video formats, providing a closer look inside the new devices.
The teardown confirms the battery capacities for the eSIM-only models:
- iPhone 18 Pro: 4,288 mAh (+0.8% vs. 4,252 mAh for iPhone 17 Pro)
- iPhone 18 Pro Max: 5,567 mAh (+9.4% vs. 5,088 mAh for iPhone 17 Pro Max)
eSIM-only models of the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max are sold in the U.S., Canada, Mexico, Japan, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain, and Kuwait. The devices have a SIM card tray in all other countries.
Battery capacities for iPhone 18 Pro models with SIM card trays surfaced previously.
The teardown also provides an in-depth look at the new variable aperture system on both models, the larger vapor chamber for cooling, and more.
NAND now sits inside the dual-layer logic board, which makes storage-related repairs less convenient, according to iFixit. In addition, the screen's plastic frame cracked or broke away on three of the four iPhone 18 Pro models it opened, which is a new issue that it did not face with previous models. However, iFixit said further testing is needed.

iFixit’s latest teardown of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max reveals increased battery capacities, a new variable aperture camera system, and significant challenges for internal hardware repairs.

### Key Points
- The iPhone 18 Pro features a 4,288 mAh battery, while the Pro Max includes a 5,567 mAh capacity, marking a 9.4% increase for the larger model.
- U.S. and several international markets receive eSIM-only versions, while other regions retain a physical SIM card tray.
- Internal cooling is improved through the integration of a larger vapor chamber across both Pro models.
- NAND storage is now embedded within the dual-layer logic board, complicating potential storage-related repairs for technicians.
- iFixit reported that the screen's plastic frame frequently cracked during the disassembly process, suggesting potential durability concerns for future repairs.

### Why it Matters
These findings highlight a growing trend where internal design choices prioritize performance and cooling at the expense of long-term repairability. As components like NAND storage become more integrated, consumers may face higher costs or increased difficulty when attempting to service or upgrade their devices.

results.title: This tiny Gmail update makes dealing with verification codes much easier
results.author: sanujb6@gmail.com (Sanuj Bhatia) , Sanuj Bhatia

What you need to know
- Gmail now shows a Copy Code button when an OTP or verification code arrives directly in your email inbox.
- The shortcut can appear inside the email and directly in the main Gmail inbox alongside the message preview.
- Google's new verification code shortcut is rolling out through the Gmail app on both Android and iOS.
Gmail now offers an easier way to copy verification codes directly from the app.
Android already makes it pretty easy to copy OTPs and verification codes when they arrive through the Messages app. But now, Google is bringing similar functionality to verification codes that land directly in your Gmail inbox.
The company is rolling out a new integration for the Gmail app on both Android and iOS that adds a small Copy Code shortcut whenever an OTP or verification code arrives.
Now, when an OTP lands in your inbox, Gmail shows a small card at the top of the email (below the subject line) containing the verification code alongside a Copy Code button. You can simply tap the button and paste the code wherever you need it, instead of manually typing it out or selecting and copying it from the email.
In addition to showing the shortcut inside the email, Gmail has also started displaying the Copy Code button directly in the main inbox alongside the email preview. That implementation doesn't seem to work every time just yet, but I've found the shortcut inside emails containing verification codes to appear much more consistently.
The feature has already started rolling out with the latest Gmail update on both Android and iOS. If you don't see it yet, it's worth updating the Gmail app to the latest available version.

results.title: Revolut Customers Targeted with New Wave of Phishing Attacks
results.author: Phil Muncaster
results.content:
Hackers have seized on a data breach at digital financial firm Revolut to try and harvest more account information from customers, according to Malwarebytes.
The security vendor said it had uncovered several examples of Revolut customers receiving smishing messages by text. One arrived on September 14, just two days after the bank acknowledged the incident.
In one example, the scam message apparently appeared in the same conversation on the victim's device as other Revolut texts, making it appear like a legitimate message.
The message urged the recipient to follow a link in order to confirm their identity, or else have access to their account restricted.
A separate customer said that opening the link took them to a web page that requested access to their device camera. Clicking “allow” reportedly initiated what appeared to be the bank’s live-video identity check, before prompting the user to enter their password.
“This makes the phishing page appear more authentic. It may also allow the scammers to collect a selfie or video that could be used for further social engineering, identity fraud, or to make subsequent scams more convincing,” wrote Malwarebytes.
“A convincing fake liveness check followed by a password screen is a common way to lower suspicion and obtain the information attackers need to attempt a real login or account-recovery flow.”
The security vendor warned that if the campaign is linked to the breach itself, rather than simply an opportunistic effort to steal account info, it could give the hackers enough info to hijack victims’ accounts.
Revolut Customers Urged to Remain Cautious
In the meantime, Malwarebytes encouraged Revolut customers to
- Not follow links in unsolicited messages, and go directly to the app if notified about an account issue
- Check the domain in the browser address bar to check it’s legitimate
- Use an up-to-date, real-time anti-malware solution on device
Details continue to emerge about the breach itself. It appears that it targeted the bank’s Lithuanian-regulated entity because it is legally obliged to respond to European Investigation Orders.
To send Revolut the fake requests for KYC information, the threat actors impersonated Italian law enforcement by compromising Italian Ministry of the Interior email accounts using infostealer logs.
They claimed to have had access to these accounts for around six months, allowing them to submit multiple fraudulent data requests without raising suspicion.
Several hundred accounts are thought to have been impacted, with high-net worth crypto users singled out for targeting after the threat actors analyzed blockchain records, according to various reports.
results.summary:
Hackers are targeting Revolut customers with sophisticated smishing attacks following a recent data breach, using fraudulent text messages to harvest login credentials and sensitive personal identity information.

### Key Points
- Security firm Malwarebytes identified phishing messages appearing within legitimate Revolut text threads, urging users to click links to verify their identities.
- Attackers utilized fake video-based identity checks to deceive victims into providing passwords and biometric data, such as selfies or video recordings.
- The initial data breach originated from compromised Italian Ministry of the Interior email accounts used to submit fraudulent information requests to Revolut.
- Reports indicate that several hundred accounts were impacted, with attackers specifically targeting high-net-worth cryptocurrency users identified through blockchain analysis.
- Revolut customers are advised to avoid clicking links in unsolicited messages and to verify account status directly through the official banking application.

### Why it Matters
These attacks demonstrate how threat actors leverage legitimate data breaches to conduct highly convincing social engineering campaigns that bypass standard user skepticism. The incident highlights significant risks for financial institutions when attackers successfully impersonate law enforcement to gain unauthorized access to sensitive customer records.

results.title: Many GOP candidates still echo Trump's 2020 claims. Lots of voters want to move on
results.author: Sam Gringlas
results.content:
Many GOP candidates still echo Trump's 2020 claims. Lots of voters want to move on
President Trump is still talking about the 2020 election — even as early voting is underway in this midterm cycle and the Republican majorities in Congress are at risk.
And while many Republican candidates, even in some critical tossup races, still back the president's baseless claims about election integrity, some GOP voters say they are ready to move on.
In Georgia, Rep. Mike Collins, the Republican nominee for Senate, launched his first congressional campaign a few months after Trump pressed Georgia's secretary of state to find enough votes to reverse his 2020 loss.
In one campaign ad from that race, Collins falsely claimed that Trump won Georgia and said, "Georgians are tired of weak-kneed, spineless politicians who won't fight for Trump, get to the bottom of 2020 and fix our elections." The spot ended with Collins firing a long gun into a bin with a "voting machine" label.
Now as Collins runs for Senate, he has reiterated his position that the 2020 election was stolen from Trump. He has also expressed support for compensating some people prosecuted for storming the Capitol on Jan. 6 to disrupt the certification of the 2020 election.
"It bothers me a lot," said Lynn, a lifelong Republican voter in Georgia, who asked NPR to publish only her first name for fear of being ostracized by friends and family for her views. "It worries me for him to get elected. It concerns me any time someone gets pulled into those ridiculous looking-back discussions."
At a farmers market in Alpharetta, a tony suburb outside of Atlanta, Lynn said she could have easily voted for the other two Republicans who ran in the primary. Now she has not ruled out voting for Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff, in part because of Collins' positions on the 2020 election.
The Collins campaign did not respond to NPR's request for comment.
Finishing a plate of grits at the farmers market, voter Austin Sapp said he regularly votes for Republican candidates, believes election fraud does happen, and supports Trump's push to pass a strict voter ID law through Congress. He also wishes the president would move on from relitigating 2020.
"It is what it is," Sapp said. "He lost, then he won [in 2024]. Beating a dead horse serves no purpose. What is your platform? What are you going to do for me?"
"Regular humans have given this up"
Just 1% of voters in a September New York Times-Siena College poll said election integrity is the top issue deciding their vote this November.
"It's really big with the media and the far edges of both parties," said Gabe Sterling, a veteran official with the Georgia secretary of state's office. "Regular humans have given this up a long time ago."
After the 2020 election, Sterling was one of the most visible officials disputing Trump's false claims. Weeks before Jan. 6, he presciently warned people could get hurt. He says that feels far from the climate now.
Sterling says while resurfacing claims about fraud can still be an effective fundraising tool, the 2020 obsession is mostly alive among die-hard activists only.
That is not insignificant though. Some of those activists now hold influential positions on state and local election boards. They also vote reliably in Republican primaries.
Sterling spoke with hundreds of GOP primary voters as he ran for secretary of state this year. He stood firm in his defense of Georgia's elections and felt like he did sway people. It was not enough to win a primary.
"I would say things like, 'Georgia has the cleanest voter list in America,'" Sterling said. "We would get some boos and hisses, but I would just keep pounding away, explaining the data and explaining what happened."
Why some candidates still back Trump's claims
In primaries elsewhere, some onetime critics of Trump's claims have come to embrace them.
In Michigan, GOP Senate nominee Mike Rogers, a former congressman who chaired the House Intelligence Committee, once called Trump's Georgia pressure campaign "more gangster than presidential," and said Trump deserved blame for the violence on Jan. 6.
But while making an unsuccessful 2024 Senate bid, in an interview with the Detroit Free Press editorial board, Rogers refused to answer who won the presidential contest in 2020. Then at a local Republican meeting last fall, Rogers claimed the Senate seat was stolen from him, according to a video of the meeting obtained by NPR.
"Now there were some ballots that showed up at 5:30, I wish I were kidding, in a van, and that swung the election on us, and it happened to be here in Detroit," Rogers said at the time.
And after Trump gave a primetime Oval Office address this summer resurrecting debunked claims about election vulnerabilities, Rogers thanked him on social media.
Rogers' 2026 Senate campaign did not respond to a request for comment.
Michigan Republican strategist Jason Roe, a former executive director of the Michigan Republican Party, says many candidates still see echoing Trump's claims as a condition for his support.
"Frankly, I think most of the elected officials that still talk about it, it's not necessarily a sincerely held belief," Roe said. "It's usually at a Republican central committee meeting, throwing red meat to the base."
Throwing red meat is likely not a strategy to win a tossup state in November, however.
"I can't imagine any Republican in a general election spending any money talking about election integrity or what happened in 2020," Roe said.
How the 2020 fixation could still shape the midterms
And yet Trump is still talking about it, potentially to the detriment of his own party's bid to keep their majorities.
In Georgia, Trump declined to endorse a Republican alternative to Collins preferred by popular GOP Gov. Brian Kemp. One reason Trump cited was that candidate correctly saying Trump lost Georgia in 2020.
A similar scenario played out in the Texas primary, where Trump endorsed the controversial state attorney general, who backed his 2020 claims. That candidate ousted Republican Sen. John Cornyn, who was seen as more formidable in the general election.
"I think we should talk about 2026 and not 2020," Cornyn told reporters this summer.
The president said this year he will do "anything necessary" to ensure the U.S. has "honest" elections.
He nearly brought legislating in Congress to a standstill earlier this year over his demands for more voting restrictions through the SAVE America Act, as Republicans tried to reopen the Department of Homeland Security. Trump has also attempted to take unprecedented control of the voting process.
Georgia's Sterling sees one motivation behind Trump's continued focus on elections.
"It distracts from the Iran war, it distracts from the Epstein files," he said. "And this is the ground on which they want to fight."
A September poll by the University of California San Diego found that only 49% of Americans expect that the upcoming midterm elections will be free and fair — lower than before the 2024 election.
Sterling says Trump seems to be laying groundwork to deflect blame if Republicans lose. If that happens, claims about rigged elections could find an audience once again.
results.summary:
Many Republican candidates continue to echo Donald Trump’s baseless 2020 election claims, creating a potential political divide as some voters express a desire to move toward future issues.

### Key Points
- Republican Senate candidates like Mike Collins in Georgia and Mike Rogers in Michigan have publicly reiterated claims that the 2020 presidential election was stolen.
- A September New York Times-Siena College poll indicates that only 1% of voters consider election integrity to be the primary issue influencing their midterm vote.
- Strategists suggest that candidates often repeat these claims to secure Trump’s endorsement or appeal to die-hard activists during primary elections.
- Some lifelong Republican voters are reconsidering their support for candidates who focus on past election results rather than current policy platforms.
- Election officials, including Georgia’s Gabe Sterling, note that while the rhetoric persists, it is increasingly disconnected from the priorities of the general electorate.

### Why it Matters
The continued focus on the 2020 election risks alienating moderate voters in critical tossup races, potentially jeopardizing Republican efforts to maintain congressional majorities. This strategy highlights a growing tension between the party's base-driven primary politics and the broader concerns of the general voting public.

results.title: The Weakest Leg
results.author: Remy Porter
results.content:
On July 10 2026, a life insurance company called TruStage had a "cybersecurity incident". According to an update posted five days later, when they revealed the incident, they are "continuing to work carefully and urgently to understand the facts, and the company will communicate appropriately as its understanding of the situation evolves."
This work, according to their outage page (last updated on September 11th, at the time of this writing), is continuing. Every major business function is listed as "partially available". They have some text explaining that they can't simply turn the system back on, because safety.
They don't know what data was compromised. They don't know when they'll have everything back up. As of mid-August they had gotten so far as setting up a "clean" environment that they could start migrating services to. The only good news is that some of their services are supplied to credit unions for banking, and those were on different systems, so only their insurance packages were compromised. I also suspect the fact that they serve credit unions is the only thing keeping the business afloat, because failing to handle transactions for months seems like a terminal event for most businesses.
Obviously, this also means they're embroiled in an ever growing number of lawsuits from a variety of parties. It also highlights something about how insurance works: it's middlemen all the way down.
TruStage will issue policies, but their connection to the actual policy holder will likely be routed through a number of different partners. Like, for example, Ethos.
Ethos uses "AI" to "democratize" insurance. Feed your data into their AI, and in minutes they'll pair you up with a policy. Which, while using machine learning to do things like assess insurance risk seems like a pretty reasonable idea, in this age of AI hype, one has to wonder how this actually is implemented and how it works in practice.
But Ethos isn't the end of the chain! Other companies live downstream from Ethos, for example, Family First Life. A customer might reach out to FFL to get a policy, FFL reaches out to Ethos (or one of many other partners), and Ethos reaches out to one of its partners (TruStage being one of their largest), and boom: an insurance happens. Like I said, it's middlemen all the way down.
But now, here's the problem: TruStage issued a bunch of policies, and then stopped being able to do business. They stopped being able to do even vital things, like process payments. And you know what happens when payments aren't made on a life insurance policy? It lapses. It goes away. You no longer have insurance. And the agents who sell those policies are often paid a commission based on the value of the first few months of the policy's life (since life insurance is expected to be a long term investment). If the policy lapses, those commissions vanish, companies like Ethos (or downstream partners like FFL) get chargebacks on the value of those failed policies.
This makes some people, like FFL's President, Shawn Meaike, very unhappy.
What we have here is a pretty egregious failure of cybersecurity and disaster recovery on the part of TruStage. It's an embarrassing and potentially terminal event for them. It's awful for the customers who bought insurance policies to give themselves peace of mind, only to discover their policies lapse because TruStage can't take their money. It's creating mild chaos in the entire industry. That's all interesting, but not why I wanted to write an article about this. I wanted to write about the incredible cringe.
In this clip from an insurance industry conference, Meaike brings up all of their partners for a "carrier panel". He then proceeds to line them up from stage right to stage left, ranking them as "weakest" to "strongest". Ethos, who sells TruStage policies, is labeled as the weakest.
"You have the weakest leg," he says, pointing at the reps from Ethos, to laughter from the audience, and then indicates the other side of the line represents "the strongest leg." Meaike hands the microphone to an Ethos employee, Dylan Cummings, "We'll start with you."
"I want to start out by thanking everyone," Cummings says.
Meaike cuts him off. "Hey, hey, hey, hey. I'm gonna help you. Why don't you start by saying you're sorry."
The crowd yells out, "Yes!" and applauds this idea.
"Say 'We have a carrier that's shut down'," Meakie continues, "'and I'm mother-freaking sorry.'"
Yes, he said "mother-freaking", on stage.
So let's recap. An insurance company gets pwned so hard they can't run operations for months. People's policies lapse, simply because they can't give their money to the insurance company. Which 100% sucks for those customers, though at least with life insurance we expect very few of them are missing their payout- hopefully! This chain cascades through the network of partners, until it culminates in the president of one company publicly humiliating the senior account manager at a middleman company, during an industry conference.
Nobody comes off looking particularly good here, obviously. Meakie is a jerk. TruStage is institutionally incompetent. Ethos is in a bit of a rock-and-a-hard-place situation, and Cummings is trying to do his best to tap dance his way out of oblivion, but it seems like the AI driven insurance startup just isn't a good partner even before their main issuer died.
All in all, it feels like a Tim Robinson sketch, or perhaps a Nathan Fielder bit. We're one step away from Meakie calling Cummings a "Wizard of Loneliness."

results.title: UN says AI safeguards can’t wait for certainty
results.author: Robert Hart
results.content:
Governments need to rein in increasingly capable AI agents before their risks are fully understood, a United Nations scientific panel warned in the global organization’s first major assessment of OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face earlier this year.
UN says AI safeguards can’t wait for certainty
The report lands as Beijing and Washington prepare to discuss AI and world leaders gather in New York this week.
The report cements AI’s place on the global diplomatic agenda this week as leaders gather in New York for the UN General Assembly and the US and China hold talks on AI. Last week, UN secretary general António Guterres called on governments to cooperate on addressing the threats posed by AI, warning that “the world cannot afford a race to the bottom on AI safety.”
It is the first thematic brief from the Independent International Scientific Panel on AI, established last year as the UN’s “first global scientific body on Artificial Intelligence.” It calls for much greater attention and resources to manage emerging risks from advanced AI, alongside stronger international coordination on safety and accountability, even as individual countries take different legal approaches.
Crucially, the panel says the world does not need to wait for scientists to establish exactly how or why such incidents occur to begin implementing stronger safeguards. Loss-of-control risk, the panel argues, is exactly the kind of problem the precautionary principle was designed to address: “one where potential harm may be catastrophic or irreversible, even as its likelihood remains scientifically uncertain.”
The principle, first enshrined in the 1992 UN Rio Declaration on Environment and Development, says that scientific uncertainty is no excuse for delaying measures against potentially serious or irreversible harm. It has since become influential in environmental and public health policy, particularly in the European Union.
Since the Hugging Face hack was first reported, incidents have been documented at companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, including hacks on real-world targets and swarms of agents taking over online messaging boards.
results.summary:
A new United Nations scientific panel report urges global governments to implement immediate AI safety safeguards, citing the potential for catastrophic risks despite ongoing scientific uncertainty regarding technology.

### Key Points
- The Independent International Scientific Panel on AI released its first thematic brief calling for stronger international coordination on safety and accountability.
- The report emphasizes the precautionary principle, arguing that governments should act against irreversible AI risks even before their exact causes are fully understood.
- Recent security incidents have impacted major AI firms, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Meta, highlighting vulnerabilities in current systems.
- The findings arrive as world leaders convene for the UN General Assembly in New York to discuss global AI governance and diplomatic cooperation.
- US and Chinese officials are scheduled to hold bilateral talks regarding AI safety and policy during the current diplomatic summit.

### Why it Matters
This report elevates AI safety to a top priority for international diplomacy, signaling a shift toward proactive global regulation rather than reactive policy. By framing AI risks under the precautionary principle, the UN is pushing for standardized safety measures that could significantly influence future legal frameworks and corporate development standards worldwide.

results.title: Toronto Dispatch: The War Against Memory
results.author: Michael Sicinski
results.content:
Words mean things, but that meaning is always changing. Sometimes those changes are organic, a gradual movement that is driven by the changing needs of speakers. But sometimes those changes are engineered from above, to serve the needs of those in power. After years of algorithmic censorship, we now see words like “unalive” or “le$bean” replacing their antecedents even in conversation, even if only ironically. (As if to prove the point, the plot of the new film by Denis Côté, Nobody’s Violence, manages to hinge on the issue of assisted suicide without ever uttering the s-word. It’s as if the film anticipates the language that will be deleted from many online reviews.) It is an embarrassing cliche to describe an authoritarian gesture as Orwellian, but using technology to eliminate words and concepts from our consciousness cannot really be described in any other way.
The word “memory” has undergone a significant shift over the past twenty years. Do you remember memory? More often than not, people now use the word to describe the capacity for digital storage, not the human ability to recall people, things, and events. This evolution seems quite deliberate. Virtually every innovation by Big Tech works to externalize the memory of the world, to delete it from our brains and store it somewhere where it can always be erased, should it become troublesome. Tools for convenience, when designed for the profit of the few, inculcate habits that dull our minds. But more than this, the offloading of consciousness onto the digital realm sets the stage for whole-cloth revisionism. Digital knowledge does leave a trace, a footprint deep in the code, but it is legible only to a select few. But it isn’t a palimpsest. A fully digital archive lacks reminders, the partial erasures and strikethroughs and overwriting, that one finds in physical culture, as well as in our memories. Instead, it allows for a wholesale find/replace function – instantaneous, possibly permanent change. (One man can rename a body of water for petty, jingoistic reasons, and suddenly, there is it.)
So memory, if shared, is a site of resistance. But of course there are many different ways to externalize memory. Artwork is one such way. It allows humans to memorialize facts and objects, thoughts, and experiences that are inconvenient, to actively prevent erasure and to share evidence among and between human minds, away from the top-down imperatives of late capitalist meaning-making. In this sense, an artwork can serve as an alternative archive, collating histories and ideas for preservation. Artworks often exist within institutions, which include museums and film festivals like the Toronto International Film Festival (TIFF). These institutions sometimes gatekeep, but crucially they also preserve. In addition to preserving individual art objects, they can also make space, preserving the very possibility for sustained attention. Right-wing strategist and former filmmaker Steve Bannon has described the need for reactionary political actors to “flood the zone,” to bombard the populace with more information, and more horror, than it is possible to mentally assimilate. This is a process that militates against memory by fragmenting attention. But artworks have a unique ability to focus our attention, to create a clearing for analysis and understanding. Art can be higher ground, a beachhead from which to establish new tactics.
In recent years, many experimental film works have exhibited an archival impulse. This has taken different forms, including the documentary exploration of archival processes, as seen in Jessica Sarah Rinland’s films, or the exploration of personal histories as a form of material culture, something we find in films as diverse as Payal Kapadia’s A Night of Knowing Nothing (2021), Sophy Romvari’s Still Processing (2020), and the work of British-Nigerian artist Onyeka Igwe. And of course Chronovisor (all films 2026 unless otherwise mentioned), one of the year’s most fascinating films, is about the research process, the accumulation of clues from old documents and dusty tomes, as a way to present contra-power histories that may have been hiding in plain sight.
Wavelengths, TIFF’s programming section for unconventional, artist-driven filmmaking, has long been an oasis for what Scott MacDonald has called “a critical cinema,” works that interrogate social structures as well as the conditions of their own making. In a variety of ways, many of the films presented in TIFF’s 2026 Wavelengths edition engage with the question of memory and the archive. Some of them, like Mariano Llinás’s brilliant, sprawling biography of Jorge Luis Borges, are in part about the process of delving into the archives and unearthing meanings that can only be derived from material history. Much of Life of Jorge Luis Borges (all titles 2026 unless otherwise noted) consists of Llinás and literary scholar Ernesto Montequín examining manuscripts and ephemera in order to piece together exactly how Borges became a transformative figure in world literature. In addition to traveling to places that were significant in Borges’s development—a library, a café, a hotel, a city block—we see the two men comparing artifacts to the descriptions of them that Borges wrote in his work. A children’s book with drawings of tigers (not by Borges, alas), or a literary magazine with a jade-green cover (alluded to in the story contained therein), and dozens of handwritten drafts are all rigorously examined, as Llinás films Montequín’s excitement as if they were making an unboxing video for YouTube. The Borges papers exemplify the seductions of the archive, showing that no matter how well you know a given subject, it is always possible to be surprised and amazed.
While some archival records augment and amend our knowledge of figures we already know quite well, others stand as evidence of otherwise ordinary lives. The commitment to archival exploration as a means of historical retrieval is seen most vividly in Electric Fragments No. 1: Rom (Uomini) (2001) by the late filmmaking team of Yervant Gianikian (who passed away this July) and Angela Ricci Lucchi (who died in 2018). Rom (Uomini) is one of a series of short films that exemplify the couple’s filmmaking ethos. They collected home movies, official government films, and other cinematic marginalia in order to consider the cultural history and ideologies contained therein. Their method could scarcely be simpler: present the film as-is, apart from slowing it down, tinting it, and adding an unobtrusive soundtrack.
As opposed to numbers two and three in the Electric Fragments series (which deal with colonialism in Vietnam and the covert sexualization of women in public, respectively), Rom (Uomini) is gentle and offers the viewer lowkey revelations from a not-so-distant past. It is taken from home movies shot in a Romani camp in Italy, and as the subtitle tells us, we are simply watching human beings: a family playing around outside, acting silly, and loving each other. One refrain in the film is the image of a baby sleeping on the ground, and a man, presumably the child’s father, placing his fedora over the baby’s face to shield them from light and noise. Gianikian and Ricci Lucchi understand that this footage is both unremarkable and priceless, probably one of the only extant records that these people and their community ever existed. It is to the great credit of Wavelengths’ programmers, Jesse Cumming and Andréa Picard, that they showcase older, underseen films like this one, along with the TM, a lyrical 1974 work by Japanese Fluxus composer Takehisa Kusogi.
Among the other films playing in Wavelengths, the political potential of the archive is demonstrated most unequivocally in Yuula Benivolski’s debut feature, The Black Box Is Orange. Composed like an essay film but also incorporating diaristic elements, Black Box finds the Russian-born Canadian returning to her childhood of Shlomi, a rundown border town in Israel. Benivolski uses her own family photos along with official military images to articulate how Shlomi was built on the land that was once the Palestinian village of al-Bassa. The Israelis have done everything they can to erase al-Bassa, but its material existence persists, in disused railroad tracks, a concrete slab in a forest, and the continued existence of a building that has withstood decades of sustained ordnance.
In her own family photos, as well as images found in the archives of Israel’s Ministry of Defense, Benivokski compiles evidence of al-Bassa’s existence. Benivolski identifies a single home on a high hill, one she remembers from her childhood and that keeps appearing in both family snapshots and official military images. In a place where the landscape is constantly being destroyed and rebuilt in order to erase any traces of Palestinian life, this structure remains like a silent witness. In its combination of personal memory and official records, this chapter of the film, titled “The Little White House,” recalls the best work of Harun Farocki or the documentary work of Israeli filmmaker Amos Gitai.
“The Little White House” would be one of the year’s best films on its own. But Benivolski surrounds it with different kinds of discourse, with the viewer asked to consider how these registers of information bounce off one another. In one segment, Benivolski tells the story of a Palestinian family whose home is repeatedly raided. Handful by handful, the soldiers steal pictures from the family’s photo album, and Benivolski learns that the Israeli Ministry of Defense contains a massive archive of such stolen photos, classifying them according to their own internal categories. As we see a series of still images of Palestinians and Israelis going about their lives (which includes the frequent wearing of gas masks), Benivolski asks us to consider the dehumanization implicit in this disciplinary archive.
While Belivolski’s film is explicitly political, there are, of course, more idiosyncratic forms of memory, ones in which the sociopolitical meanings remain implicit. Some films are less concerned with producing an objective record than in generating a visceral impact by looking at the world in unusual ways. Such films are records not of the thing itself, but the affective relationship between the filmmaker and their subject. In a sense, what is meant to be preserved is the experience of looking at a person, place, or thing. Johann Lurf’s hypnotic Forever…Forever is a record on one very specific place in Austria, the Ottenstein Reservoir in Austria. For this 20-minute film, Lurf shot footage from the exact same angle for nearly two years. There is a body of water in the foreground, a bridge over the water, and two shores covered in trees.
Forever…Forever is the type of film that could hypothetically be made anywhere. If you pay close enough attention to a given place for a long enough span of time, it is inevitable that changes will occur: changes in season, in light, in activity. But as Lurf demonstrates, the reservoir is a unique location. It represents an engineered space that contains water, an artificial construction in the landscape. From his chosen angle, Lurf fills most of the frame with water and the reflected sky. The bridge is dead center, like a bowtie holding the image together. Using time-lapse photography, Forever…Forever details the cycles of time as observed from this single spot. The sun rises, it sets, the moon comes out, and it sets in turn. The trees accumulate snow, their leaves change. Using an accelerating timeframe, as the timelapse increasingly condenses more time into fewer 65mm film frames, Lurf presents a document of what the naked eye cannot see. Much like Michael Snow’s La région centrale (1971) or certain films by the late Tomonari Nishikawa, Forever…Forever is a testament to deep observation. It shows us that any place participates in the general, cosmic movement of the planet while also maintaining its radical particularity.
Like Lurf’s film, two short films in the program pay close attention to very specific objects, suggesting the ways that people go about preserving cultural heritage against destruction. Mustafa Uzuner’s The Address Book is a simple film that shoots the pages of an address book, in order, one after the other. The method recalls Hollis Frampton’s filmed script Poetic Justice, or better yet Heinz Emigholz’s page-by-page presentation of his notebooks in the Basis of Make-Up series. The Address Book preserves a delicate object and offers it for display. Specific names and numbers tell us that the book’s owner is part of the New York art world, but when we learn that it belonged to Joseph Cornell, an additional layer of meaning emerges. Cornell, after all, exemplifies the artist as magpie, collecting and assembling nondescript bits of detritus and memorabilia in sculptural showcases. Uzuner’s film performs much the same function. Cornell was a filmmaker as well as a sculptor, composing his works using excerpts from science films, newsreels, and, in the case of his most famous film, Rose Hobart (1936), clips of the titular actress from her role in East of Borneo (1931). Uzuner combines these tendencies, “encasing” Cornell’s personal artifact on celluloid.
La Prospettiva (1653) by Ben Russell is a gentle observational recording of the process of physical preservation and upkeep. The film gazes down the length of the Colonnade at the Palazzo Spada in Rome, watching carefully as two workers clean the dust from its arch and walls. This is one of Russell’s simplest and most poetic films, recalling Friedl vom Gröller’s cinematic haikus of European life. Drawing on the vernacular of structural films like Serene Velocity (1970) and, indeed, Wavelength (1967), Russell optically takes us into the colonnade, turning the portico into a bounded yet infinite space.
As the title tells us, Russell is considering the way that Baroque space, designed by Borromini, plays tricks with our perception, tweaking the Albertian optics of the Renaissance and making the space less rational, more haptic and experiential.In a way, La Prospettiva forms an intriguing diptych with Russell’s other film from this year, Another Earth. That film is organized around a blitz of doomscrolling on an iPhone, imparting a sense of claustrophobia and despair. The phone, after all, takes all of human life and reduces it to the consumable optics that photography inherited from the Renaissance. By contrast, La Prospettiva tells us that certain things can endure for centuries, that the world contains great mysteries, provided there are people willing to care for them.
One of the festival’s most powerful films, Ghazal-e Sorkh by Maryam Takafory, speaks very directly to the engineering of memory through public spectacle as well as active suppression and destruction. Where Takafory’s recent films have involved a feminist and queer counter-reading of the history of Persian-language cinema, Ghazal-e Sorkh engages with governmental propaganda, specifically the cult of personality around Iran’s last shah, Mohammed Reza Pahlavi. Framed around the story of her own father’s arrest for attending a protest in 1974, Takafory’s film details the mass suppression of books and authors under the Shah’s dictatorial rule, which he was able to wield in no small part due to the support of Western capitalist nations. Takafory tells the viewer about others who protested in 1974, including a group of young women poets who were killed. Ghazal-e Sorkh does not need to remind the viewer of the 2022 murder of Mahsa Amini by Iran’s morality police. The film trusts us to recognize that fascism takes many forms but that misogyny remains constant.
Takafory goes on to list numerous books that were banned by the Shah’s cultural institutions, noting the reasons given for their suppression. As always, the forces that engage in censorship understand what “free speech” liberals conveniently forget. Words are dangerous, and books represent the precarious archive of revolutionary speech. Takafory has prepared a damning document that memorializes both the Shah’s tyranny and the West’s political and financial incentives for ignoring it, particularly when compared with the demonizing of the 1979 Shia revolution. We see the Shah’s lavish, decadent birthday celebration, attended by fawning heads of state from around the world. And as a final, poignant twist of the knife, Takafory interpolates fragments from the Shah’s propaganda film, Flame of Persia (1971), narrated by none other than Orson Welles. The message is clear: no one, no matter how politically astute, is above being lured astray by flattery and money.
Archival knowledge is unstable, something that must itself be guarded from attack. Generative AI doesn’t simply erase human history. It is used to create deceptive histories out of decontextualized sounds and images. A film that speaks directly to this, 09/05/1982, premiered in the 2025 Wavelengths program and was one of the most important films of last year. In it, directors Camilo Restrepo and Jorge Caballero present supposed documentary footage, both audio and video, of the violent aftermath of an unrising in an unspecified Latin American nation. As the film continues, anomalies accrue and eventually we realize we’ve been duped. The filmmakers used generative AI to fabricate very convincing archival evidence of a historical event that never took place. 09/05/1982 is precisely about the danger posed to historical knowledge, including material artifacts of the past, by tools that have been designed to inculcate false consciousness. A similar point is made, although in a somewhat different register, by Danaya Chulphuthiphong’s Microcosmic Orbit: Encased, from this year’s program. Where Restrepo and Caballero demonstrate the possibility of media manipulation, Microcosmic Orbit is about the artificial preservation of the natural world, which can also entail manipulation and deception.
Beginning with shots of people swimming in a lagoon, Chulphuthiphong uses close-ups and distorted angles to confuse the viewer regarding what we are actually seeing. Some of the plants and mosses we witness are artificially grown, kept in terrariums. As with several other films discussed above, Microcosmic Orbit takes us behind the scenes as workers in a natural history museum organize and arrange plants, rocks, and lichens to produce exhibits that mimic “nature” but are not in fact natural formations. Chulphuthiphong reveals the process whereby “nature” is manicured, manipulated, and preserved. The irony is that “nature” would not be an object to preserve were it not for the human race’s endless reshaping of the earth, and the eradication of the very flora on display in this natural history museum.
In a sense, the exhibition space in Microcosmic Orbit presents the natural world like an argument: edited, assembled, and exhibited as a metonym, an example of something beyond itself. Chulphuthiphong also demonstrates the ways that cinema can participate in this argumentative process. This is a vital reminder. Memory isn’t neutral. It is subject to engineering, even by seemingly benign institutions. As so many of these films demonstrate, archival knowledge is partisan because those instigating enforced forgetting are also partisan. Filmmakers, then, must become archivists, because archivists represent a guerilla force in the war against memory.
results.summary:
The 2026 Toronto International Film Festival’s Wavelengths program highlights how experimental filmmakers use archival techniques to preserve human memory against digital revisionism, algorithmic censorship, and state-sponsored historical erasure.

### Key Points
- The Wavelengths program features films like *Life of Jorge Luis Borges* and *The Black Box Is Orange* that utilize archival research to challenge official narratives.
- Filmmakers such as Yervant Gianikian and Angela Ricci Lucchi employ "archival impulses" to document marginalized lives, including Romani communities in Italy.
- Works like *09/05/1982* and *Microcosmic Orbit* explore the dangers of generative AI and artificial preservation in distorting historical and natural truths.
- The program emphasizes the role of cinema as a "guerilla force" that protects collective memory from the top-down imperatives of late capitalism.
- Featured directors include Mariano Llinás, Yuula Benivolski, Johann Lurf, and Maryam Takafory, who each interrogate the intersection of personal history and institutional power.

### Why it Matters
In an era of digital find-and-replace functions and algorithmic content moderation, the act of preserving authentic history has become a radical form of resistance. These films demonstrate that memory is not a neutral record but a contested site where artists must actively intervene to prevent the wholesale erasure of inconvenient truths.
